11-alice-s-adventures-in-wonderland:
A bored girl follows a waistcoated rabbit down a hole and lands in a world of odd rules. Lewis Carroll's Alice's Adventures in Wonderland began as a tale told on a river trip. Twelve chapters carry Alice through tears, keys, doors, and talking beasts.

She meets the Caterpillar, the Cheshire Cat, the Mad Hatter, and the Queen of Hearts. Size shifts, riddles, and croquet with flamingos test her logic at every turn. The book ends with a trial over stolen tarts. Its wordplay made it a lasting classic for children and adults alike.
19761-a-girl-in-ten-thousand:
A Girl in Ten Thousand is a story for girls by L. T. Meade, a prolific writer for young readers. Its heroine is dark-eyed and sweet-faced, though her words can sound hard. She might be any age between seventeen and twenty. Meade's girls usually face school, work, or family trials. One in ten thousand is the praise her worth must earn.

Meade wrote hundreds of books for girls in her lifetime. Her stories mixed school life with moral tests and romance. Readers followed heroines who worked, studied, and held their ground. This novel fits that popular pattern. It shows what Victorian and Edwardian girls were offered as models. The charm is period charm, preserved whole.
19799-the-rural-motor-express-to-conserv:
The Rural Motor Express was a wartime plan to move farm goods by truck. Its stated aims were to conserve foodstuffs and labor and help win the war. The argument runs on efficiency: highways must be used to the maximum. Motor trucks can run where no fixed rail lines exist. They can also relieve railroads of short-haul loads. Trucks would act as feeder lines in thinly served districts.

Food rotted when rail cars ran short in wartime. A truck route from farm to town saved both crop and car space. Federal and state groups pushed the express idea in 1918. This pamphlet is their sales pitch and manual. It marks the moment trucks joined national transport planning.
19806-everyman-s-land:
C. N. and A. M. Williamson wrote Everyman's Land as a postwar travel romance. Its speaker confesses to wanting hatred and misunderstanding. He disguised himself as a Leprechaun and sulked, he admits. It did not work with the one person who understood him. She taught him people are much the same all over the world. The voice is whimsical, wounded, and confessional at once.

The Williamsons wrote bestselling travel novels between the wars. Everyman's Land crosses Europe's battle-scarred lands. A fairy-tale mask lets the narrator say hard things lightly. The lesson he learns is the book's thesis. Travel here heals a man the war left bitter. It is a gentle, strange period piece.
19822-with-the-british-army-in-the-holy-:
Henry Charles Woods wrote With the British Army in the Holy Land about the Palestine campaign. He opens with the land's long war history. Palestine was the cock-pit of the known world before Belgium held that name. Egyptians, Assyrians, Israelites, Canaanites, Greeks, and Romans fought there. Saracens and Crusaders followed on the same high road. The British Army of 1917 marched into that deep past.

Allenby's campaign took Jerusalem and broke Ottoman rule in Palestine. Campaign histories appeared while memory was fresh. Woods writes for readers who followed the war in newspapers. Sacred geography and modern logistics fill the same chapters. The book is a primary record of that campaign. It also shows Britain framing conquest as history.
19928-sunset-pass-or-running-the-gauntle:
Sunset Pass promises a run through the gauntlet of Apache land. A captain in its pages thinks first of the children. Renegades from the reservation are out in great numbers, he says. They are supposed to be down in the Tonto Basin. Yet their moccasin tracks have shown up nearby. Charles Seltzer wrote such Arizona westerns with a working cowboy's knowledge. Fear rides every mile of this one.

The Tonto Basin was real Apache country, steep and ambush-ready. Seltzer's novels pit settlers and soldiers against that terrain. Tracks in dust carry more dread than gunfire here. Sunset Pass belongs to his early, lean westerns. It shows the genre before Hollywood standardized it. Local detail is its claim on readers.
19966-the-statesmen-snowbound:
The Statesmen Snowbound is a comic tale of congressmen trapped by weather. Its narrator pleads the sacrifices congressmen make to serve the nation. They give up home life, business interests, and personal comforts, he says. Yet unthinking persons begrudge them a little pleasure. Snow gives the statesmen that pleasure by force. Robert Grant, a Boston judge and novelist, wrote the satire. Washington marooned makes his whole joke.

Grant first published the tale in the 1880s, and it stayed famous. Snowbound politicians must amuse themselves without constituents or press. Their stranded leisure exposes pomposity and boredom alike. The piece is gentle Thackeray-style satire, American style. It also preserves Gilded Age political manners. Few Washington comedies have lasted as well.
20043-the-angel-children-or-stories-from:
The Angel Children, or Stories from Cloud-Land, tells tales for young readers about child life and loss. One girl, Genevieve, has a large playroom full of fine toys. Other children think she must be perfectly happy with so much. Yet she would trade it all for a little brother of her own.

Genevieve longs to walk in the garden with a brother and watch over him. Her mother watches her in just that caring way. The tales blend home life, faith, and gentle moral lessons. They show what children's books of the era taught about love and want.
20057-pocket-island-a-story-of-country-l:
Charles Clark Munn published Pocket Island in 1901, a story of country life in New England. The sample turns to the Maine coast and the rum trade. Rum was cheap in Nova Scotia and dear in Maine. That gap made smuggling liquor a risky but rich trade.

Munn knew Maine life well and set much of his work there. Inside, coast folk, traders, and law men move around hidden cargo. The tale mixes local color with crime and cash. Readers get a sharp look at a coast where work and smuggling often sat side by side.
20068-sarah-s-school-friend:
May Baldwin wrote Sarah's School Friend, a girls' school story set in a London home. Mrs. Clay speaks in a strong cockney voice, with dropped h sounds. She scolds Sarah, a girl of sixteen, for sharp talk at home. Sarah has called her mother a humbug and slighted her father.

That clash opens a tale of school, family, and a young girl's pride. Baldwin wrote many such books for girls of her day. Inside, friendship tests Sarah's temper and her sense of right. Readers get period speech, home friction, and the pull of a school friend's sway.
20226-snow-bound:
Snow-Bound gathers writing shaped by winter, storm, and the fireside. Its opening verse comes from Emerson on the arrival of snow. Announced by all the trumpets of the sky, the snow arrives. It seems nowhere to alight as it drives over the fields.

The whited air hides hills, woods, river, and heaven from sight. Sled and traveler stop, and housemates sit by the radiant fire. Such scenes made snowbound tales a loved winter form in New England. Readers get poems and prose that turn deep winter into warm company.
20288-edward-the-second:
Christopher Marlowe wrote Edward the Second, a history play of a weak king's fall. Edward asks why the Lord of Coventry hurries so fast past him. The bishop replies that he goes to mark the old king's funeral. But wicked Gaveston has returned, the bishop protests in alarm.

Edward vows that Gaveston shall live to be revenged on the priest. Gaveston was the king's favorite, and his exile had been forced by barons. Marlowe turns their bond into a tragedy of power, pride, and revolt. Readers get one of the great early English history plays in verse.
20311-the-bobbsey-twins-on-blueberry-isl:
Laura Lee Hope published The Bobbsey Twins on Blueberry Island in 1917. Bert sits beside his sister Flossie in a boat on Lake Metoka. He says he is hungry yet, despite having eaten not long before. He wants some of Dinah's pie, but he also wants to stay out longer.

That small choice sets the twins' holiday mood of fun and appetite. Blueberry Island gives the four Bobbsey children a camp to explore. The series blends twins, lakes, and gentle mysteries for young readers. Readers get sunny days, boat rides, and pie worth rowing home for.
20467-handbook-of-the-trees-of-new-engla:
Lorin L. Dame's Handbook of the Trees of New England is a field guide to the region's native and planted trees. It covers New England, with notes on ranges across the United States and Canada. Keys and descriptions help readers name a tree in any season.

Dame warns that near the limit of a species, size and habit change a great deal. In trees this change is often very noticeable. He also notes there is no fixed, absolute line between trees and shrubs. Such cautions make the handbook a careful tool, built for people who would test every name outdoors.
20522-the-story-of-the-mind:
The Story of the Mind is a popular survey of psychology, the science of how minds work. Its author thanks the magazines that first printed parts of it. Passages came from the Popular Science Monthly, the Century Magazine, and the Inland Educator.

The Macmillan Company and the owners of copyright also gave their leave. That list shows how the book was built: short, clear chapters first tested on magazine readers. It covers memory, feeling, instinct, and thought for people with no training. Books like this one carried the young science of psychology into ordinary homes.
20588-the-wonder-island-boys-exploring-t:
Roger T. Finlay's The Wonder Island Boys: Exploring the Island, published in 1914, continues his series about boys cast away on a strange island. The boys explore with a friendly professor's help, and every chapter teaches real skills along with the adventure. Their finds raise as many questions as they settle.

The contents promise an arrow found in the skull of an animal, and notes on different kinds of arrows. There is a light across the river, the test of firing a gun, and the disappearance of the light. The boys also learn the qualifications in scouting. Curiosity drives every chapter.
20625-young-americans-abroad-vacation-in:
Young Americans Abroad records a vacation in Europe by a party of American youths, told in letters home. The travels run through England, France, Switzerland, and Italy. Letter writing was the natural form for travel books aimed at young readers of the time.

I have just arrived at this place, one letter begins, and have found my companions on hand. All are ready for the start of the long-hoped-for voyage. The writer regrets the duties that keep their friend at home, and says all feel sorry for the absence. The letters mix sights, history, and boyish fun.
20712-trail-s-end:
G. W. Ogden's Trail's End is a Western novel of the Kansas plains after the cattle years. Its opening paints the prairie as a graveyard of hopes. Bones lie everywhere: a waste of bones, a sepulcher that does not hide its bones but spreads them to bleach under the stern sun.

They are bones of deserted houses, the skeletons of men's hopes, crumbling on sterile wastes. Into that emptied country Ogden brings his riders and ranchers, men and women chasing a second chance. Ogden knew Kansas newspaper life, and his West is drier and harder than the dime novel kind.
20885-the-promised-land:
A little girl's world once split in two: Polotzk, where she lived, and a strange land called Russia. Mary Antin opens The Promised Land with that child's sharp map. Russia was where one's father went on business, far and dim.

Antin tells how her Jewish family left Polotzk for Boston and a new life. School, English, and hard work remake her across the book's famed arc. Her memoir became a classic tale of the immigrant's road in America. Few books state the hope and cost of that change with her clarity, pride, and eye for telling detail.
20897-a-short-history-of-england:
Britain is less an island than a maze of peninsulas, says G. K. Chesterton. Sea in the fields and fields in the sea strike the eye at every turn. A Short History of England opens with that edgy, bright paradox.

Chesterton retells England's tale as a story of the common folk. Romans, Normans, kings, and revolts pass in his brisk, witty prose. He skips dry lists to chase the spirit of each age. First issued in wartime 1917, the book still charms readers who want history with a pulse, told by a master of the telling phrase.
21003-bell-s-cathedrals-the-cathedral-ch:
Thanks to the Rev. Perkins and the Photochrom Company open W. D. Sweeting's Ely Cathedral guide. Their photos ground the plates that walk readers through the great church. Loans of rare, out-of-print books aided his history of the monastery and see.

Bell's Cathedrals paired sound text with fine photos for church lovers. Ely's nave, lantern, and lady chapel star in Sweeting's calm account. He sorts tangled building tales into clear, dated order. The book served as pocket guide and home study alike, a trusted mate for one of England's grandest churches.
21069-for-treasure-bound:
A November gale at Weymouth opens Harry Collingwood's treasure novel, told by a young hero who shares the author's pen name. His father never came back from a voyage and is presumed lost at sea. Hints point to a treasure island somewhere in the Pacific.

A beautiful, fast cutter is built for the search, and Collingwood writes the shipyard scenes with a working shipwright's eye. The party sails for the Pacific and meets adventures on the way. A charming young woman joins the voyage, and the hero falls in love. Treasure, family loss, and sea travel drive the tale.
21085-the-wreck-of-the-nancy-bell-or-cas:
John Conroy Hutcheson's Nancy Bell sails from Britain for New Zealand in good order, then meets a storm that leaves her rudderless and mastless. Among the passengers travels a former Royal Navy commander in disguise. He offers the captain advice, which is brushed aside as a landsman's talk.

A mutiny breaks out before the ship is wrecked off Kerguelen Island in the far southern ocean. The survivors land, build shelter, and face a hard winter there. Hutcheson gives his Jamaican, Irish, American, and Norwegian characters their own speech. The castaways must also deal with the mutineers who landed apart from them.
21132-frank-oldfield-lost-and-found:
Langhurst, a mining village in south Lancashire, opens the Reverend T. P. Wilson's temperance novel, published in London in 1872. A collier with his Davy lamp meets Alice, a woman whose looks have been scorched away by drink, searching for her boy Sammul. Drink and the pit rule the village's hard life.

Wilson wrote for the Band of Hope movement, which taught children never to start drinking. Frank Oldfield's story of being lost and found plays out among colliers, drinkers, and those trying to save them. The novel won wide circulation as a prize temperance tale, mixing dialect speech with a clear moral purpose.
21198-anecdotes-of-painters-engravers-sc:
S. Spooner was a doctor who also wrote a biographical history of the fine arts. He packed this second volume of anecdotes with lives and curiosities of art. It opens with Titian: his manners, works, imitators, and his dealings with Emperor Charles V and Philip II. A sketch of Horace Vernet follows.

Later pieces range over the Colosseum, the remains of Nineveh, a palace dug up at Nimroud, and the ruins of Pompeii and Herculaneum. The origin of the arch, ancient fresco and mosaic, and the Portland Vase all get entries. Published in New York, the volume serves as a lively miscellany for art lovers.
21245-three-boys-in-the-wild-north-land:
Mr Ross welcomes three sunburnt boys to Sagasta-weekee, his house full of sunshine on the Nelson River, in Egerton Ryerson Young's tale. Frank, Alec, and Sam have sailed by the Prince Arthur to York Factory on Hudson Bay. Ross, a retired Hudson's Bay Company officer, hosts them in his hunting lodge.

The boys spend a season of adventures in the wild north land. They meet Inuit travellers and learn the country from a man whose father also served the Company. Young had worked as a missionary in the region and wrote from experience. Hunting, travel, and winter coming on give the three visitors their education in the North.
21246-winter-adventures-of-three-boys-in:
A November storm rages outside while Frank, Alec, and Sam sit at breakfast in a cosy northern home in Egerton R. Young's sequel. The three boys came from Britain the previous summer by Hudson's Bay Company ship and stayed on as guests of Mr Ross. Now winter, their first in the great lone land, is the adventure.

Dog teams, whips, and the dog keeper Kinesasis start the season's lessons. Ross had spent his career in the fur trade on friendly terms with the Indigenous peoples around him, and his household keeps that closeness. Snow travel, hunting, and the long dark shape a winter the boys will not forget.
21284-six-years-in-the-prisons-of-englan:
An unnamed merchant tells how he began business in a northern city in 1856. He paid his creditors in full after a failed partnership, and still ended in prison. Frank Henderson edited the account, first printed in Temple Bar Magazine and reissued in London in 1869. The author writes for a kind brother who cheered his darkest hours.

Chapters follow his feelings on entering prison, his trial and sentence, three months in a Scottish prison, and removal to a Yorkshire one. Fellow prisoners fill the pages: an old jail bird, a soldier, an innocent convict, and a cracksman planning murder and escape. Victorian prison life is shown from a cell.
21321-before-the-dawn-a-story-of-the-fal:
Joseph A. Altsheler set this 1903 novel in Richmond as the Confederacy falls. It opens on a raw, gusty morning. A thin, brown-faced officer with a stiff left arm and a bullet-holed uniform boards a train for the capital. Chapters move through the Mosaic Club, the Secretary's manoeuvres, and a woman in brown pursued through the city.

Robert and Lucia carry the love story through the pall of winter, while the chapters on feeding the hungry show a starving capital. Altsheler knew the Civil War deeply and wrote many novels of it. The fall of Richmond ends an era for his characters, in flight, fire, and change of flags.
21357-nic-revel-a-white-slave-s-adventur:
Nic Revel grows up on a small Devon estate where poachers keep raiding the family's salmon pool. In George Manville Fenn's tale, a big fight at the pool ends with Royal Navy men supporting the Revels. Wounded in the dark, Nic is mistaken for a poacher and press-ganged with the men he fought.

Carried to America still half conscious, he is sold by the ship to a slave dealer. The dealer sells him on to a settler far up a river in alligator land. Hard work and poor food follow for Nic and a poacher turned friend. Their long effort to escape and reach Devon again drives the tale's second half.
21391-great-african-travellers-from-mung:
Finding the sources of great rivers drove the men in W. H. G. Kingston's Great African Travellers. The book runs from Mungo Park to Livingstone and Stanley, the best known names in African travel. At the start of their age, the coasts were mapped, but the deep interior was not.

Kingston tells how each traveller set out from a coastal base and won leave to pass inland. Some African rulers gave a warm welcome, and others did not. The Nile and its twin branches drew many of the boldest trips. The book gives a clear, joined account of a whole age of bold travel.
21393-hendricks-the-hunter-or-the-border:
Hendricks earns his living by the gun in W. H. G. Kingston's tale of Zululand, Hendricks the Hunter. He hunts game and trades skins and other goods along the border farms. The book opens among the steep ranges and deep valleys of South Africa.

One long hunting trip carries the action, told with Kingston's usual care for place. Wild beasts, snakes, and thirst are constant threats on the trail. The Zulu people he meets are drawn with warmth when they prove friends. A heavy wagon, built of stink wood, hauls the loads. The tale mixes trade, travel, and danger in equal parts.
21416-randy-of-the-river-or-the-adventur:
Randy Thompson works his way up from the river bank in Horatio Alger's Randy of the River, published in 1906. Randy is a patient fisher who waits at the hole while other boys wander off. That same steady grit marks all his dealings in the tale.

As a young deckhand on a river boat, Randy meets greed, blame, and unfair charges. In one key scene he tells Mr Polk that a loss was not his fault, and he will not stand for it. Alger's hero holds to honest work and a clear name. The tale rewards him in the usual Alger way, by steady rise.
21458-charley-laurel-a-story-of-adventur:
Charley Laurel passes into a sailor's hands as a small child in W. H. G. Kingston's Charley Laurel. At a West Indian place just attacked by the British, his nurse is fatally wounded. Seaman Dick Driver takes the boy and raises him aboard ship.

Their luck runs wild: cast away on a raft, picked up by pirates, saved by a privateer. On a South Pacific island, captors hold the two apart. Charley's trick frees Dick, and a British ship takes them off. In England a shipowner's family takes to the boy and sends him to school.
21489-the-secret-of-the-island:
W. H. G. Kingston translated Jules Verne's The Secret of the Island from the French. The tale follows a party cast away on a Pacific island after a balloon trip. Kingston also gave English readers a version of The Swiss Family Robinson.

Pirates and escaped convicts from Australia trouble the settlers' hard-won home. At odd times, unseen help saves them, as if some power watched over the island. That power proves to be Captain Nemo, hidden in a vast cave with his wealth. The book stands as a sequel to Twenty Thousand Leagues Under the Sea.
21579-snarleyyow-or-the-dog-fiend:
Snarleyyow, the dog fiend, survives every attempt on his life in Captain Marryat's novel of 1837. Frost coats the spars and small iron guns of his ship at dawn. All hands but his owner treat the ugly beast with spite, and he returns the favour.

Marryat sets the tale when a Dutch-born king sat on the English throne. His Dutch courtiers and officials fill the court, and the cutter runs often to the Netherlands. Side plots breed in those crossings, among a crew of hopeless, unkind folk. The dog outlasts them all, as nasty at the end as at the start.
21591-the-harbours-of-england:
John Ruskin writes on Turner's ports in The Harbours of England, given here from his complete works. Turner and the engraver Lupton began the Ports of England as a serial in 1826. Only three numbers appeared before the plan stalled for want of time.

Ruskin's text, first issued in full in 1856, treats Dover, Ramsgate, Plymouth, and Portsmouth. Margate, Falmouth, Sidmouth, Whitby, Deal, and Scarborough follow in short, rich chapters. Collectors paid eleven or twelve guineas for proof sets of the plates. The editor laments that Ruskin's readers have passed the book by, and this edition makes the case anew.
21721-the-coral-island:
Ralph Rover tells his own story in Ballantyne's most famous book, a tale of boys cast away on a South Sea island. Ralph was born at sea, the son and grandson of captains, and roving runs in his blood. He ships out as a boy, hungry for adventure in foreign lands, and a wreck gives him more than he asked for.

On the island, Ralph and his companions must find food, build shelter, and face dangers from sea and land. Ballantyne never saw the Pacific, yet his coral shores and lagoons convinced generations of readers. The book shaped nearly every island adventure written after it, and boys read it eagerly for a century.
21729-dusty-diamonds-cut-and-polished-a-:
London street children stand at the center of this Ballantyne novel, first published in 1884. Two homeless boys near Whitechapel, in the East End, are taken off the streets by rescuers. They are trained up and sent to Canada, to live with a farmer's family there. Their story runs beside a grimmer one.

The mother of one boy struggles with drink, too many children, and a violent, thieving husband. Her eldest daughter holds the family together while the father sits in jail. Ballantyne drew the title from his theme: rough lives hold worth that care can polish. The tale gives a close look at street life in the London of his day.
21732-fort-desolation-red-indians-and-fu:
Jack Robinson is the plain, quiet hero of this Ballantyne tale of a lonely fur-trade fort in Rupert's Land. To strangers he looks like the most commonplace of men, sandy-haired and unnoticed. In truth a deep stream of romance runs in him, flashing out only in rare moments. Solitude does not suit him, yet his work gives him plenty of it.

Ballantyne sets the story among the traders and native peoples of the far northern wilderness. He knew that world from his own Hudson's Bay years in Canada. Trade, travel, and the long winters of an outpost shape the tale. Jack's calm grit holds it together from first page to last.
21826-my-pet-recipes-tried-and-true-cont:
Favorite dishes of a church circle fill My Pet Recipes, a Canadian cookbook gathered by the ladies and friends of St. Andrew's Church in Quebec. Each recipe comes as a pet of its giver, tried and true in her own kitchen. The pages carry the marks of their time and place. Furs by Holt, Renfrew are advertised at the front, and grocers promise the freshest goods in Quebec.

Community cookbooks like this one preserved home cooking that no chef ever wrote down. Soups, cakes, and preserves pass from neighbor to neighbor in print. The ads around the recipes are part of the record too, showing the shops those cooks relied upon. For food historians, such books are gold: plain, practical, and close to real tables.
21948-little-busybodies-the-life-of-cric:
Insects get biographies in Little Busybodies, a nature book for children aged eight to fourteen. Jeannette Marks and Julia Moody of Mount Holyoke College published it in 1909. The life of crickets, ants, bees, beetles, and their kin is told as story-led science. A journey to Rangeley Village frames the lessons. Chapters march with the little army of grasshoppers, listen to cricket fiddlers, and ask how Katy did with the katydids.

Dragonflies go fishing, and may-flies live their brief day in the telling. The book belongs to a Harper series covering crabs, shells, fish, birds, and flowers in the same plan. Pictures name the cast, from cicada killer to mole cricket. It teaches close watching as a form of fun.
22108-the-untroubled-mind:
Herbert J. Hall, a doctor who treated nervous patients, wrote The Untroubled Mind about worry and restless living. Hall warns that peace will not arrive in a flash of revelation. Change comes slowly, by returning again and again to honest work. He refuses to belittle that struggle; he wants it fought at a better level.

His counsel joins medical sense to a quiet faith in purposeful occupation. Ordered work, outdoor life, and simple interests steady the mind in his practice. The book grew from Hall's work with invalids who had lost their trades. It is an early, humane entry in the literature of mental health, still readable for its calm good sense.
22142-the-modern-scottish-minstrel-volum:
Charles Rogers, a Scottish minister and antiquary, edited The Modern Scottish Minstrel. Volume V continues his gathering of Scotland's songs with lives of the song-makers. The series aimed to carry Scottish song from Burns's age into Rogers's own century. Each song comes with notes on its author and its air.

This volume's opening matter praises bodies that relieved poor men of genius and learning. Such societies kept Scotland's literary spirit alive, Rogers believed. Portraits of the poets face their songs. The Minstrel volumes are quarries for anyone studying Scottish song: words, tunes, and biographies together. Volume V holds the later letters of the alphabet of poets.
22201-the-butterfly-s-funeral-a-sequel-t:
The Butterfly's Funeral continues the insect world made famous by The Butterfly's Ball. That tiny verse fable, written for the Roscoe children, had charmed Georgian England. In this sequel the butterfly is dead and must be buried in state. The corpse is embalmed at sunset and enclosed in a case spun by the silkworm herself.

The hornet helps lay the coffin on a bier of myrtle and jasmine. Beetles, bees, and all the ball's bright company form the funeral train. The poem teaches children nature's names through pageantry and grief. Such miniature books, printed for the nursery trade, were the picture books of their day, and this sequel kept a beloved trifle alive.
22210-in-the-forbidden-land:
A. Henry Savage Landor travelled in Tibet when Tibet was closed to foreigners, and In the Forbidden Land tells how. Landor was captured, tortured, and expelled by Tibetan officials in 1897. His two-volume account caused a sensation on its release. Reviewers quoted in the book praise its vivid verbal pictures and the author's own drawings and photographs.

Landor describes passes, monasteries, and the men who hunted him across the plateau. He presents himself as artist and explorer in one, emphasising the letterpress with his pencil. Some contemporaries doubted details; the adventure's core was never in question. The book remains a classic of forbidden-frontier travel writing.
22229-the-modern-scottish-minstrel-volum:
Volume VI closes Charles Rogers's Modern Scottish Minstrel, his great gathering of Scotland's songs. Rogers pairs each song with the life of its maker. This volume's frontispiece shows Paisley, birthplace of Tannahill, Alexander Wilson, and John Wilson. Weaver poets and Paisley shawls stand behind many of these songs.

Rogers opens with a reflection on poetry as the first language of nations. The lyric muse, he writes, chose lands of mountain and flood, and left them when liberty died. The songs that follow, with their notes, prove his devotion to that idea. Six volumes strong, the Minstrel remains a working library of Scottish song and song-makers.
22342-supermind:
Supermind is a science fiction story preserved from Project Gutenberg, again featuring Malone. He agrees peacefully with whatever the Director of the FBI says. He eyes that powerful man with due wariness.

After all, Malone argues, the news is nothing new. The country has always been going to hell in a handbasket. One way or another, he says, decline is the old story. That shrug sets the tale's tone of dry humor under pressure. A supermind, by the title, stands behind the trouble. Readers get a wry period story where vast powers and federal men meet one unflappable talker.
22377-rollo-in-switzerland:
Rollo in Switzerland sends a young American traveler through the Alps. Rollo was the hero of a famous series of travel books for children. His last day in Paris opens this volume's journey.

In Paris, Rollo learned the passport system by actual experience. That lesson in paperwork readied him for crossing into Switzerland. The series taught geography through a boy's questions and mishaps. Adults in the books explain countries, customs, and rules as they go. Young readers toured Europe without leaving home. This Swiss volume offers mountains and manners together. It shows how nineteenth-century families taught travel, order, and curiosity in one small package.
22581-the-child-voice-in-singing-treated:
Francis E. Howard wrote The Child Voice in Singing, a teaching treatise published in 1895. Howard treats the child's singing voice from both a bodily and a practical angle, with special care for girl and boy choirs. His audience is the large body of vocal music teachers in public schools.

Howard argues that the core of all vocal teaching must be brought home to school instructors in a convincing way. He holds that teachers accept a new idea only when its truth is proved to them plainly. The book therefore mixes body science with classroom argument. It remains a useful window on how singing was taught, and how reformers tried to change school music from inside.
22590-wind:
Wind is a science fiction story with a Dutch flavor, set partly around Earth's seas and partly on Venus. The catalog record names no author and gives no year. Its dialogue name-checks the IJsselmeer and the old Zuider Zee, and its sailors speak like men used to rough water and tall claims.

In the sample, a captain named Heemskerk teases young Jan about returning punctually, broom at the masthead and all, the old sailor's sign of a swept, victorious sea. Jan answers that brooms are scarce on Venus. The blend of sea lore and space travel marks the tale's playful spirit. It offers readers a short, salty mix of nautical tradition and planetary adventure.
22756-the-enchanted-island:
The Enchanted Island is a children's fantasy issued by E. P. Dutton and Company in 1919. The catalog record credits the publisher. Its world is an archipelago of four big islands, each a separate kingdom that has nothing to do with the others, ripe ground for a young traveler's adventures.

The largest island is called the Island of Sunne because it is the nicest and has the finest weather. It never rains there in the daytime, but only at night, which, the narrator admits, is very convenient. That confiding voice, half guide-book and half fairy tale, carries the story from kingdom to kingdom. The book belongs to the shelf of gentle wonder tales written between the wars, when enchanted islands still dotted children's maps.
22765-lynton-and-lynmouth-a-pageant-of-c:
Lynton and Lynmouth: A Pageant of Cliff and Moorland is a topographical book about the twin villages of north Devon and their wild coast where Exmoor meets the sea. The catalog record names no author and gives no year. Pageant is the right word: the book parades the district's history, legends, and scenery in order.

Up and down the length of England, the text reflects, lie traces of far-off peoples. They run from Land's End to the Northumbrian dales. Their very names are faint guesses kept only in local speech. Around Lynton those traces run through cliff, combe, and moor. The Valley of Rocks, the East Lyn river, and smugglers' tales all take their turn. Such books served walkers in the great age of British hiking, and they keep the local lore that guidebooks now shorten.
22972-rollo-in-holland:
Jacob Abbott explains Dutch dikes in Rollo in Holland. The dikes are so immense, and so covered by houses, trees, mills, and even villages, that a traveler first seeing them can hardly believe they are dikes at all. Some run several hundred feet wide, with a broad public road on top and a canal beside it.

Rollo's Holland tour follows the Abbott formula, questions from the boy, patient answers from his elders, and a whole country turned into lessons. Windmills, canals, and tidy towns supply the sights. The series taught American children geography by pretending to travel with them. Its Holland remains a fair picture of what educated tourists admired there, order, industry, and land won from the sea.
23090-yr-ynys-unyg-or-the-lonely-island:
A Welsh title crowns Yr Ynys Unyg, or The Lonely Island. Its narrator settles business briskly. The action took place close enough to home, she says, that a stranger would have little difficulty recognizing the heroes and heroines mentioned. As the narrative begins very abruptly, she will first give some personal account of the parties concerned.

An island, a household cut off from the world, and a woman's retrospective voice give this old tale its shape. The book descends from an eighteenth-century Welsh novel tradition, part romance, part conduct tale. Solitude tests its people's tempers, faith, and affections in turn. Readers meet a rare survival, Welsh fiction in English dress, preserved here under its bilingual title for anyone tracing the novel's spread beyond London.
32-herland:
Three male explorers stumble on a hidden land run entirely by women. Charlotte Perkins Gilman's Herland, told by one of the visitors, imagines a society that has raised children without men for generations. The narrator writes from memory, his notes lost.

The visitors test the land's schools, gardens, cities, and mother-centered faith. Their assumptions crack as the women answer with calm logic and order. Romance grows, but so does debate about freedom and sex roles. The novel stands as a sharp early work of feminist utopian fiction. Later feminist writers returned to Gilman's island as a model for imagining fairer societies.
322-st-ives-being-the-adventures-of-a-fr:
Robert Louis Stevenson dictated St. Ives to his stepdaughter Mrs. Strong between January 1893 and October 1894. The tale, in its 1898 Heinemann second edition, follows a French prisoner in England during the Napoleonic wars. Stevenson laid it aside six weeks before his death.

Thirty chapters bring the tale within sight of its end, and Mrs. Strong knew the intended remainder in outline. A completion by another hand follows for readers who dislike unfinished stories. The adventure mixes escape, romance, and prison life. St. Ives shows Stevenson's late storytelling power. Stevenson's unfinished tale still grips readers of adventure fiction.
324-a-knight-of-the-cumberland:
A narrator leads his small sister and a city girl called the Blight up a Cumberland gap. John Fox Jr.'s Knight of the Cumberland opens at high noon on a crisp October day, with a gray horse and two mules. The party climbs where few women but mountaineers have trod.

Contents follow the blight in the hills, a wild dog's trail, and a tournament at last. Fox writes mountain folk with local color and romance. The knight of the title proves his worth in a closing passage. The book shows Fox's Kentucky mountains at their most vivid.
505-history-of-the-warfare-of-science-wi:
Andrew Dickson White traces the long clash between science and church dogma in this two-volume history, combined here. From creation to evolution, from comets to medicine, White shows how literal readings of scripture blocked inquiry, then slowly gave way. Ezra Cornell, co-founder of Cornell University, receives the dedication.

White writes as a historian and university builder, marshaling cases with calm, learned force. His ice-barrier image opens the book: truth presses like spring water till old walls break. The work endures as a landmark plea for free inquiry, and for a faith that need not fear fact.
51-anne-of-the-island:
Anne Shirley leaves Green Gables for college in this third Anne book. Lucy Maud Montgomery's Anne of the Island follows Anne to Redmond College with friends old and new. Letters from home, Patty's Place, and first proposals fill her terms.

Gilbert Blythe waits in the background while other suitors press their cases. Anne learns what she wants in work, friendship, and love. The novel closes with spring and a return to the island. It bridges Anne's schoolgirl years and her adult life. Montgomery balances college comedy with quiet scenes of home, loss, and growing resolve.
586-religio-medici-hydriotaphia-and-the-:
Thomas Browne meditates on faith, death, and friendship in this volume of three seventeenth-century works, edited by J. W. Willis Bund. Religio Medici sets out Browne's personal religion with learned wit; Hydriotaphia, or Urn Burial, reflects on Roman urns dug in Norfolk; a Letter to a Friend counsels a sick man.

Browne writes in vigorous, rugged prose, a tissue of many tongues, as Johnson later put it. His style strikes more than it soothes, yet it rewards slow reading. The book serves as a classic of English meditation, where a physician-philosopher weighs belief against the grave.
649-ancient-poems-ballads-and-songs-of-t:
Robert Bell edits this collection of old English poems, ballads, and songs of the peasantry, gathered from broadsides and oral tradition. The Plain-Dealing Man, The Vanities of Life, and The Life and Age of Man lead the poems. Ballads follow, like The Three Knights, The Blind Beggar of Bednall Green, and The Bold Pedlar and Robin Hood.

Bell's notes place each piece in its folk setting, from harvest to highway to churchyard. The verses speak of work, love, death, and jest in plain, sturdy lines. The volume serves as a treasury of English folk verse, where the voice of common people survives in song.
666-the-gutenberg-webster-s-unabridged-d:
This section of Webster's Revised Unabridged Dictionary, published in 1913 by Merriam under Noah Porter, covers words beginning with P. Entries give spelling, pronunciation, part of speech, etymology, and numbered senses, from P, the sixteenth letter, through Pa, a short form of Papa, and Paage, a toll for passage, and onward. Notes trace Latin, Greek, and Phoenician roots.

P is a letter of passages and payments: tolls, papers, and parcels fill its early pages, with plants and proverbs close behind. The entries show how prefixes like pa- and pre- built whole families of words. For a reader of old law, letters, or trade, this slice is a practical key.
699-a-child-s-history-of-england:
Charles Dickens wrote this history of England for young readers, in plain, story-like prose. It runs from ancient Britain and the Romans through Saxon kings, the Norman conquest, and the long line of later monarchs. Each chapter takes a reign or an age and tells its chief events as a tale, with heroes, villains, and turning points.

Dickens speaks straight to children, praising good kings and blasting cruel ones, and he does not hide his views on power and pride. The book was meant to give the young a first, vivid sense of their country's past. It still reads as a lively, if partisan, tour of English history, and as a window on how Victorians taught that past.
717-chita-a-memory-of-last-island:
Lafcadio Hearn wrote this tale of Last Island, a pleasure resort off Louisiana that a great hurricane swept away. A small girl named Chita is found after the storm, alone among the wreck, and taken in by a Creole household. The book opens with the legend of the island, then follows Chita's rescue and her new life.

Hearn writes the Gulf coast with lush, musical prose, full of sea, heat, and Creole custom. Beneath the beauty lies the storm's terror and the fragility of a gay, careless world. The book is both a memorial to a lost place and a tender story of a child saved from the sea, told by a master of atmosphere.
754-the-story-of-mankind:
Hendrik Van Loon wrote this history of the world for young readers, from early man to his own day. He tells the story in short, vivid chapters, with maps and drawings by his own hand, moving from Egypt and Greece through Rome, the Middle Ages, and the modern age. His voice is that of a lively teacher, not a dry scholar.

Van Loon links great events to the lives of ordinary folk and to ideas that changed the world, from writing to steam. The book won the first Newbery Medal and taught generations their first world history. It still charms as an old-fashioned, humane tour of mankind, even where later research has revised its facts.
858-stage-land:
Jerome K. Jerome wrote this comic guide to the world of the stage, as seen by the earnest student of the drama. He sorts stage folk into types: the hero, the villain, the heroine, the comic man, the lawyer, the adventuress, and the servant. Each type behaves by fixed rules that real life rarely follows.

Jerome mocks the gap between stage manners and common sense, with jokes on swoons, asides, and sudden fortunes. His dedication, to that retiring student of the drama, sets the teasing tone. The book delights theatre lovers, for it names every cliché they have laughed at, and it still reads as a witty tour of Victorian melodrama.
883-our-mutual-friend:
Charles Dickens wrote his last completed novel about John Harmon, heir to a fortune in dust heaps, who is supposed drowned on his return to London. The Boffins, his father's servants, inherit instead, and the tale follows their rise, the Wilfer family, and the river folk who found Harmon's body. Money, marriage, and murder intertwine.

Dickens fills the novel with rogues, lawyers, and schoolmasters, and with the Thames as a dark mirror of the city. Lizzie Hexam, Bella Wilfer, and Bradley Headstone carry a story of love and obsession. The book stands as a rich, sombre masterpiece, and a fitting close to Dickens's great career.
885-an-ideal-husband:
Oscar Wilde wrote this play about Sir Robert Chiltern, an ideal husband and rising statesman, whose past holds a secret sale of a state secret. Mrs Cheveley, a schemer with a letter as proof, blackmails him, while his wife, Lady Chiltern, holds him to a standard no man can meet. Lord Goring, the witty friend, must save the day.

Wilde's dialogue dazzles, but the play turns on forgiveness: Lady Chiltern must learn that ideals need mercy. First staged in 1895, the play was a triumph before Wilde's fall. It remains a brilliant comedy of politics and marriage, where wit and feeling share the stage.
a-child-s-history-of-england:
Charles Dickens wrote this history of England for young readers, and the contents show its march reign by reign. It begins with ancient England and the Romans. It passes the Saxons and Alfred, then the Normans and the Conqueror. From there it goes through the Plantagenets: Henry the Second, Richard the Lion-Heart, John Lackland, and the long line of Edwards and Henrys.

Dickens tells each reign as a story of character — proud kings, wicked uncles, battles, and murders in towers — with his sympathies plainly engaged. He admires Alfred and Edward the First, scorns John and Richard the Third, and treats the Tudors and Stuarts at the same brisk pace, ending with the later Stuart kings. The history was written to be read aloud in a family, and its judgments are a novelist's, not a scholar's.
a-daughter-of-the-land:
Gene Stratton-Porter opens in a small country church, where the minister takes his text: take the wings of morning. Outside, tall Kate Bates bends low along the footpath to keep her head below the windows. She is the youngest of a land-rich, cash-poor family, and the land that should have been her portion has gone to her brothers.

Twenty-eight chapters follow Kate through teaching, a contract quarrel, courtship, marriage, and the long work of winning a farm of her own, ending with blue ribbon corn. Chapter titles like Kate Takes the Bit in Her Teeth state her character plainly. Stratton-Porter writes farm life from inside knowledge, in praise of work and independence.
a-history-of-the-early-part-of-the-reign:
Charles James Fox's History of the Early Part of the Reign of James the Second, printed here in Cassell's 1888 National Library edition, is the great Whig orator's unfinished monument. Fox collected his materials in Paris in 1802, after the Peace of Amiens, and worked on the history in his last years. He died in 1806; the book appeared in 1808. It begins with his view of Charles II's reign and ends with Monmouth's execution in 1685, the early part only, as the title honestly warns.

Fox writes as a parliamentarian judging a king who meant to rule without parliaments. James's designs on the army and the law are traced from inside Whig memory. Sedgemoor and the Bloody Assizes end the fragment in tragedy. Readers get two books in one: a primary voice of English liberalism, and a history of 1685 written by the statesman who most feared its lessons being forgotten.
a-journey-to-the-western-islands-of-scot:
Samuel Johnson left Edinburgh on August 18, 1773, with James Boswell, to see the Hebrides he had long wished to visit, as his opening pages tell. This text follows the 1775 edition with the 1785 corrections. Johnson crosses the Firth of Forth to Inch Keith and works north along the coast before turning to the islands.

He records inns, roads, lairds, language, second sight, and the remains of the clan world after its breaking. Johnson judges schools, churches, and poverty with his usual force, and praises what earns praise. The book is travel writing of a high order: sturdy, curious, and full of sentences built to last.
a-knight-of-the-cumberland:
John Fox, Jr. wrote this short novel of the Cumberland mountains. That is the coal and feud country along the Kentucky and Virginia line. The narrator leads his small sister and a fashionable young visitor on horseback. The visitor is nicknamed the Blight. They cross the crest of the Big Black mountain. Their goal is country of moonshiners and feudsmen, where, he says, an older way of life still holds. The contents list eight chapters.

The visitors meet mountain customs head-on. They join a wild dog hunt. They pass a shooting scrape at close quarters. Election day counts as a great day. At last comes a tournament in the old style, where local men ride as knights. The Blight's presence tests both worlds. Fox made the Cumberlands his subject, and wrote the tale as both romance and report.
a-prisoner-in-fairyland:
A Prisoner in Fairyland is a 1913 novel by Algernon Blackwood, one of the most prolific writers of ghost stories in the history of the genre. Blackwood, also a journalist and broadcasting narrator, earned high praise from critics of the weird tale. Here he turns from ghosts to fairyland, and traps his hero among the fairies in an odd, gentle fantasy.

The mortal man dwells in the enchanted realm as a captive, and the story unfolds softly rather than as a tale of terror. Blackwood's gift was for atmosphere, for the thin border between the everyday world and a stranger one beside it. This novel applies that gift to fairyland, making captivity itself a dreamlike state the reader drifts through.
addresses-by-henry-drummond:
Henry Drummond's spoken addresses open with Love, the Greatest Thing in the World, his famous talk on the thirteenth chapter of First Corinthians. He asks what the supreme good is, and answers against the common view: not faith, but love, is the greatest thing. The contents add Lessons from the Angelus, Pax Vobiscum, and First, an address to boys.

Later talks treat the changed life and dealing with doubt. Drummond, a Scottish scientist and evangelist, spoke to students across Britain and America, and his manner here is plain, warm, and direct. The love address alone was printed in huge numbers and carried his name around the world.
aesop-fables-townsend:
Aesop, a storyteller of ancient Greece, gave his name to hundreds of short animal fables. George Fyler Townsend translated the full body of tales into English prose. Foxes, hares, tortoises, and farmers crowd his pages.

Each brief story ends by teaching its lesson plainly. The tortoise beats the hare, and the boy who cried wolf loses his flock. Townsend's version became the standard English Aesop for generations of children. Adults still quote these morals without knowing their source. Few books so short have shaped so much everyday wisdom. Townsend's edition first appeared in 1867 and was reprinted many times.
afoot-in-england:
W. H. Hudson's Afoot in England opens by refusing guide-books, in a chapter that introduces his own. Hudson counts England's guides by the library and finds them never out of date, only superseded. On Going Back and Walking and Cycling state his method: slowly, on foot, returning. Seeking a Shelter and Wind, Wave, and Spirit follow.

Roman Calleva and a cold day at Silchester explore the buried Roman town under Berkshire fields. Salisbury and its doves, Whitesheet Hill, and Stonehenge with its tillage fill the Wiltshire chapters. In Praise of the Cow honours the animal of the downs. Hudson, the Argentine-born naturalist, walked England as an exile in love with a second home. His prose lingers where guide-books hurry: a road leading nowhere, an Abbotsbury swannery, a river followed for its own sake. The book is a classic of English walking.
algonquin-legends-of-new-england:
Charles G. Leland tells in his preface how the work began in the summer of 1882 among the Passamaquoddy at Campobello. He expected scanty remains of heathenism there. He found instead a whole mythology kept by oral tradition. His book gives the myths and folk lore of the Micmac, Passamaquoddy, and Penobscot tribes, as the title page states. A birch-bark frontispiece shows Mikumwess, the Indian Puck.

The contents center on Glooskap, the great hero: his birth, his making of elves, men, and beasts, his deeds, his family, and his battles with sorcerers and giants. Leland prints the tales with notes comparing Norse and other traditions. The collection preserved stories that might otherwise have been lost within a generation.
alice-s-adventures-in-wonderland:
Lewis Carroll wrote this children's novel about Alice, a girl who follows a waistcoat-wearing White Rabbit down a rabbit hole. She lands in a world that runs on nonsense and wordplay. The contents list twelve chapters, from the fall itself through the pool of tears, the caucus-race, and the mad tea-party, to a final trial over stolen tarts.

Alice grows and shrinks, argues with a Caterpillar, and meets the Cheshire Cat and the Mock Turtle. She also plays croquet with a flamingo under the Queen of Hearts, who orders heads off at every turn. Carroll plays with logic, verse, and riddles all through. The book's dream logic and puns made it a landmark of children's literature, read by adults as much as by children.
an-ideal-husband:
Oscar Wilde's play centers on Sir Robert Chiltern, a respected government official whose career rests on a secret from his youth. The cast list places the action in his London house and in Lord Goring's library. A visitor, Mrs. Cheveley, arrives holding proof of the old wrong and demands a price for her silence.

Four acts mix drawing-room wit with blackmail, a stolen brooch, and a friend who seems lazy but thinks clearly. Lady Chiltern must weigh the perfect husband she imagined against the flawed man she has. Wilde uses the plot to question public purity and private forgiveness, and the dialogue sparkles throughout.
ancient-poems-ballads-and-songs-of-the-p:
Robert Bell edited this anthology of the poems, ballads, and songs of England's rural poor, printed in London in 1857 as the title page shows. His subtitle states the sources: pieces taken down from oral recitation and transcribed from private manuscripts, rare broadsides, and scarce publications. The contents divide the harvest into poems, ballads, and songs.

The poems moralize on life, age, and death, with dialogues between an exciseman and Death and between husbandman and servingman. The ballads tell of Robin Hood, Lord Bateman, the blind beggar of Bednall Green, and Sir John Barleycorn. The songs praise the plough and the farmer's boy. Bell prints the material as literature worth keeping, with an introduction on its origins, preserving a working-class song culture that print was about to scatter.
angel-island:
Inez Haynes Gillmore opens Angel Island on the morning after a shipwreck. Five men lie bruised and speechless on a Pacific beach, haunted by the drowned. Frank Merrill, Honey Smith, Pete Murphy, and Billy Fairfax count their losses. No ship, no women, and no rescue are in sight.

The island's wonder arrives on wings: a company of flying women descends from the sky. The men fall in love with creatures who can leave whenever they choose. Courtship turns into a struggle over freedom, as the men plot to clip the women's wings. Gillmore, a feminist writer, built her fantasy as an argument. Angel Island uses a desert-island romance to ask who owns a woman's body and movement. Its serene prose carries a radical charge that still startles.
anne-of-the-island:
Lucy Maud Montgomery continues Anne Shirley's story in this novel, which opens with Anne leaving Green Gables for Redmond College. The dedication speaks to girls everywhere who wanted more about Anne. Forty-one chapters follow her college years: rooms at Patty's Place with friends, stories sold and rejected, proposals accepted and refused, and letters carrying news from home.

At home, Avonlea changes without her: Diana marries, old neighbors die, and Gilbert Blythe waits through Anne's confusion about what love should look like. A brief glamour with another suitor clears her mind. The final chapters bring degrees, weddings, and Anne's recognition of where her heart has been all along. The book balances campus comedy with a quiet growing-up.
bede-ecclesiastical-history-england:
Bede, a monk of Jarrow in Northumbria, finished his Ecclesiastical History of the English People in 731. The translation here is the version revised from J. A. Giles's standard English text. Bede's history is the founding work of English history, and our main source for the island's conversion.

In five books he runs from Caesar's invasion to his own day. The heart of the work is the coming of Augustine's mission from Rome, the kings who accepted or refused baptism, and the saints of the young English church. Bede's care with sources and dates set a standard few medieval writers matched. The book made the English a people with a story.
beyond:
John Galsworthy built his novel Beyond around Gyp, the daughter of retired lancer Charles Clare Winton, whose story opens at a registry office. Gyp has just married a foreign violinist her father calls the fiddler fellow, against his judgment and her own better knowledge. The marriage fails in the way Galsworthy marriages do: quietly, through temperament, selfishness, and the slow discovery that love was appetite.

What follows tests what a woman may claim beyond the rules. Gyp finds real love where the law and divorce courts of Edwardian England will not let her marry again. Galsworthy, who wrote The Forsyte Saga of property and marriage, here asks what fidelity means when the legal bond is the false one. The tone is tender and unsparing at once.
boy-scouts-of-the-air-on-lost-island:
Gordon Stuart's The Boy Scouts of the Air on Lost Island is a boys' adventure story built around flying, a dam and a mysterious island. Three boys wait at dawn in a back yard, watching for their friend Tod, while the sky lightens over the cedars.

Chapters promise a hopeless search, more thrills, a startling clue, a rescue, a voyage in the dark, and a mid-air miracle. The scouts patch their machine, the Skyrocket, and play a big game against rivals who trick them again and again. Stuart writes in the brisk serial manner of the period, and young readers who enjoy scouting tales with aeroplanes will find the pace unflagging.
brandes-main-currents-4-naturalism-in-en:
England's writers come under Brandes's eye in the fourth book of Main Currents, here in English, under the head of naturalism. He traces the turn toward plain truth in fiction and verse. A Dane's view of Victorian letters can startle English readers even now.

Brandes praises force and honesty while faulting prudery and cant. He sets English books beside French and German ones to test their worth. His judgments are bold, clear, and often still argued over. The volume shows how an outsider with wide reading could see a nation's writing more clearly than many of its own critics.
castle-richmond:
Castle Richmond, by Anthony Trollope, is his Irish novel of the great famine, presented here in a 1906 edition with an introduction by Algar Thorold. Thorold reports that Trollope wrote it in 1861, long after leaving Ireland, and judges the plot mechanical and the characterization weak, with one great exception. The book's value, he argues, is documentary: graphic famine scenes observed carefully and, on the whole, impartially.

The exception is Abe Mollett, an unscrupulous blackmailer drawn, Thorold says, with real art and a hunter's loving preoccupation. Around the castle and its family, Trollope sets landlords, priests, and parsons against starvation in County Cork, and the introduction notes that his priest comes off a better man than his parson. Modern readers often come to this novel for exactly what its introducer praised: a major novelist testifying, from memory and conscience, to a catastrophe England preferred to forget.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-abbey-of-croy:
The Catholic Encyclopedia entry on Croyland, or Crowland, describes a Benedictine monastery in Lincolnshire, sixteen miles from Stamford. Ethelbald, King of Mercia, founded it early in the eighth century in memory of St. Guthlac.

Danes destroyed the house and slaughtered its community in 866. After refounding under King Edred it burned again in 1091, was rebuilt by Abbot Joffrid, and burned once more in 1170 before rebuilding under Abbot Edward. Thereafter Croyland prospered almost unbroken to the Dissolution, richly endowed by visitors to Guthlac's shrine and secure in its fenland isolation. The entry names its notable abbots, including Ingulphus.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-abbey-of-mori:
The Catholic Encyclopedia entry on Morimond describes the fourth daughter of Cîteaux, in Champagne. Odelric d'Aigremont and Adeline de Choiseul founded it in 1115, with Arnold as first abbot. Arnold, its first abbot and a member of one of Germany's noblest families, was long counted a column of the Cistercian Order.

Through Arnold's zeal Morimond grew rapidly, planting colonies across France, Germany, Poland, Bohemia, Spain and Cyprus. Celebrated foundations included Ebrach in 1126, Holy Cross in 1134, and Aiguebelle in 1137, and by the late eighteenth century Morimond counted nearly seven hundred daughter houses. Briefs from popes also placed Spain's military orders under Morimond's spiritual jurisdiction.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-absalon-of-lu:
Absalon of Lund, also known as Axel, was a famous Danish prelate born in 1128 at Finnestoe in Seeland. He died at Soroe's Benedictine monastery on 21 March 1201, the house his father founded. A graduate of the University of Paris, he taught briefly at Ste. Genevieve's school. Roskilde gained him as bishop in 1158; Lund gained him as archbishop in 1178, with primacy over Denmark and Sweden, and eventually he served as papal legate.

In that office he laboured for the final extirpation of paganism in Scandinavia, notably on Rugen, its last stronghold. He held great political influence under King Waldemar I and Canute VI. At his request Saxo Grammaticus composed his sixteen books of Danish history, and the fourteenth book carries a tribute to Absalon himself.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-ancient-see-o:
Ribe, with twenty-nine deaneries and 278 parishes, covered Ribe, Vejle, and Ringkjobing, with part of North Schleswig. Saint Ansgar founded its first church in 860. Saint Rembert served it, and heathens destroyed it after his death in 888. It rose again toward 948, when Saint Leofdag, first Bishop of Ribe, was consecrated by Archbishop Adaldag of Hamburg.

Leofdag is said to have been martyred by heathens at Ribe. Until the death of his third known successor Vale, who ruled from 1044 to 1059, the bishops of Ribe, Schleswig, and Aarhus wandered Jutland on missionary tours. In 1060 Jutland was divided into Ribe, Aarhus, Viborg, and Vestervig. Bishop Thure, from 1125 to 1134, began the Cathedral of Our Lady, finished under Elias, from 1142 to 1166, who founded the chapter in 1145. Radulf, an Englishman, brought Leofdag's relics to the cathedral, though Leofdag was never formally canonized.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-antoine-galla:
Antoine Galland, a French scholar of the East born in 1646, gave Europe its first Arabian Nights. Poor after his father's early death, he won patrons who sent him to study at Noyon and Paris. At twenty-four the French ambassador took him east, where he learned Turkish, Persian, and Arabic.

As king's antiquary in the Levant, he gathered coins, inscriptions, and manuscripts for France. In 1709 he took the chair of Arabic at the College de France. His translations ranged from Indian fables to Ottoman and Persian histories, and his Nights, drawn from Arabic tales, made him famous far beyond scholarly circles.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-auckland:
Auckland is a diocese covering the Auckland provincial district of New Zealand, with its islets and the Kermadec Group, an area of 21,665 square miles. Its story opens in 1835, when Pope Gregory XVI erected the Vicariate Apostolic of the Western Pacific. He chose Jean Baptiste Francois Pompallier as its first vicar. Pompallier reached Hokianga in January 1838 with Marist fathers, at a time when fewer than one hundred white Catholics lived in all New Zealand.

Marist missions to the Maori people grew fast despite hostile rumors spread by Wesleyan trader-missionaries. By April 1846 about five thousand Maori had been baptized, with many more preparing. Pompallier moved his base to Auckland in 1845, and Auckland and Wellington were later split into separate sees. April 1906 figures close the entry: twenty-nine parochial districts, seventy-nine churches, about five thousand Catholic Maori, and two thousand six hundred children in Catholic schools.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-basutoland:
Basutoland is a mountainous district of South Africa, a prefecture apostolic of 10,293 square miles. It is bounded by the Orange River Colony, Natal, and Cape Colony, with Maseru as chief town. About 700 whites and 309,000 natives live there, ruled by native chiefs under a British Resident Commissioner. The climate is healthful, cold in winter, rainy in summer, and the country has neither railways nor proper roads.

Annexed to Cape Colony in 1871 and a Crown Colony from 1884, it became an independent prefecture on 8 May 1894. The Oblates of Mary Immaculate, present since about 1862, founded Roma, its first mission, that same year. Its first prefects were Monginoux, Baudry, and Cenez, all Oblates. Droughts, locusts, and few priests hamper evangelization, though a settled population keeps missionaries close to their flocks.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-bequests-for-:
Bequests for Masses in England receive a long legal history in the 1913 Catholic Encyclopedia. Before the Reformation, gifts of land or money for Masses were valid, save where mortmain laws barred gifts to religious houses. Tenure by divine service even bound land to prayers for the dead, and great wills of the age are full of such gifts.

The break came with the Chantries Act of Edward VI, which dissolved chantries and cast doubt on requiem Mass bequests ever since. Later statutes and court cases, including the Superstitious Uses Act, narrowed what testators could leave. The entry traces that long legal shadow from medieval piety to modern trust law.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-blessed-ferdi:
Blessed Ferdinand, Prince of Portugal, is the subject of this 1913 Catholic Encyclopedia entry. Born in Portugal in 1402, sixth son of King John I and Philippa of Lancaster, he died at Fez in Morocco in 1443. Sickly from youth, bodily weakness never hindered a spirit and intellect of remarkable quality, the entry says.

His mother had nursed a martial spirit in her sons, giving each a sword on her deathbed for widows, orphans, and country. Ferdinand joined the disastrous Tangier expedition of 1437, was left hostage for Ceuta, and died in captivity rather than see the city surrendered. The entry presents a prince-martyr of Portugal's crusading age.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-blessed-louis:
Louis Allemand, Cardinal and Archbishop of Arles, became the leading voice for council supremacy over the pope at the Council of Basle. Born near Belley about 1380, he rose through papal service to become Bishop of Maguelonne in 1418, Archbishop of Arles in 1423, and cardinal in 1426.

At Basle he headed the party that deposed Eugenius IV and elected Felix V, whom he consecrated and crowned in 1439, while also tending plague victims and promoting the Immaculate Conception decree. After Felix resigned in 1449, Nicholas V restored Allemand's dignities, and he died in 1450, venerated as Blessed from 1527.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-catholic-univ:
The plan for a Catholic University of Ireland took shape at the Synod of Thurles in 1850. Reviving true learning mattered for the well-being of Irish Catholics, and lay students needed higher schooling on Catholic lines. They kept away from the Queen's Colleges, where religion had no official recognition. Pius IX had suggested it, and Louvain offered an inspiring example.

The Holy See approved it in 1852, funds poured in, and property was bought in Dublin. John Henry Newman became rector. He took his oath of office at Pentecost in 1854. The university's work began that November under statutes sanctioned by Rome, with papal authority to grant degrees. The hierarchy, acting through a committee, governed the institution.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-christian-bro:
An entry on the Christian Brothers of Ireland, an institute founded at Waterford in 1802 by the merchant Edmund Ignatius Rice. After two centuries of penal laws, a Catholic could not legally school his children as Catholics, nor could a teacher take up the work. The ignorance and misery of Waterford's Catholic boys moved Rice to act. Bishop Hussey backed him, and in 1800 he gave his fortune and his life to the cause.

Rice opened his first school in 1802, and young men soon joined him; the citizens built them a monastery in 1803. Houses followed at Carrick-on-Suir, Dungarvan, and Cork, where the bishop summoned citizens to gain the same benefit in 1811. Dublin gained a community in 1812, and by 1907 ten Dublin communities taught over 6,000 pupils in primary and secondary schools, orphanages, and industrial schools.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-cleveland:
The Diocese of Cleveland, established on 23 April 1847, covers the part of Ohio north of the southern limits of ten counties from Columbiana to Van Wert. Its territory spans thirty-six counties and 15,032 square miles. The first missionaries in Ohio were Jesuit Fathers Potier and Bonnecamp, coming from Quebec in 1749 to evangelise Hurons along the Vermilion and Sandusky Rivers.

Two years later Father de la Richardie joined them from Detroit and settled part of the Hurons near present Sandusky, building a chapel, Ohio's first place of Catholic worship. These Hurons took the name Wyandots on leaving the parent tribe. Drawn into the French and Indian War and then Pontiac's conspiracy, they saw the Jesuits unjustly forced out in 1752, Potier the last among the western Hurons. No systematic mission work followed until 1795, when Father Edmund Burke came as chaplain at Fort Meigs near Maumee, serving there until February 1797.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-commissariat-:
Gregory Cleary's entry defines a Holy Land commissariat in the Order of Friars Minor. It is the district assigned to a commissary gathering alms for Palestine's Holy Places, kept by the Friars Minor. More narrowly it means the convent where that commissary lives. Always a friar, he takes office by letters patent from the minister general. Each year he sends the minister an account of alms received. Those alms may never, without express leave of the Holy See, go to other ends, however pious.

Bishops' annual collections reach Jerusalem's custos through their district commissary. Forty commissariats stood across the Christian world. Naples, founded when Robert of Anjou redeemed the Holy Places from Egypt's sultan, ranks as the oldest. Seven served English-speaking lands. The United States commissariat sits at Washington's Mount Saint Sepulchre, with new houses in California and Saint Louis.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-congregation-:
Ernest Salmon's entry covers the Congregation of Saint Edmund, founded in 1843 by Jean-Baptiste Muard at Pontigny, France, for popular missions. Members also give themselves to parish work, youth education in seminaries and colleges, direction of pious associations, and foreign missions. The motherhouse stands at Pontigny, but since the expulsion of religious orders the superior general lives at Hitchin, England.

In the United States the congregation holds two houses. Swanton, Vermont, hosts a missionary house and apostolic school training young men for priesthood and religious life. Winooski, Vermont, holds a college with twelve fathers, eight scholastics, and one hundred pupils. Short as the entry is, it maps a missionary congregation's French roots, English exile, and American classrooms in a single compact sketch.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-damaraland:
A mission entry describes Damaraland, the middle part of German South-West Africa between latitudes 19 and 23 south. From the Atlantic coast the traveller crosses a 42-mile sand belt of giant dunes. Next come ninety miles of barren desert with bare mountains. Then Hereroland proper rises to 7,000 feet, and finally the rolling Omaheke plain runs toward the Kalahari. Rain is scarce, and only cattle-raising thrives.

Its peoples were the Hill Damara, about 20,000 original possessors robbed of pastures by the invading Herero, and the Herero themselves, Bantu immigrants of the seventeenth and eighteenth centuries. Down to modern times the Damara lived among the Herero as slaves, but sided with Germany in the Herero rising and improved their lot. Catholic missions, schools, and the region's peoples are surveyed in turn.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-didymus-the-b:
Didymus the Blind of Alexandria was born about 310 and lost his sight at the age of four. Yet in time he ranked among the best-read scholars of his day. A Catholic Encyclopedia entry tells how he learned by listening, turning over at night what readers had read aloud by day. In time he seemed to have written it all on the pages of his memory.

Saint Jerome called him not the blind man but the Seer. Saint Anthony told him to rejoice in a spiritual sight shared with saints and apostles. The entry surveys his biblical commentaries and his place among the teachers of Alexandria. It also weighs which works are truly his, giving a vivid life of learning without eyes.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-dietrich-gres:
Dietrich Gresemund was a German humanist born at Speyer in 1477. His father, a court physician to the Elector of Mainz, gave him a thorough classical schooling. A Catholic Encyclopedia entry notes that by 1493 the youth was already linked with Wimpfeling and Abbot Trithemius. In 1494 he printed his first work, and Trithemius praised him as a youth who had outstripped many grown men, even doctors.

Gresemund studied medicine at Speyer like his father and moved in the learned circles of Mainz. He died there in 1512, only thirty-five years old. The entry gathers the scant sources for a short life that still shows how early German humanism prized Latin letters and new learning.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-education-of-:
Blindness and its teaching are the subject of this long survey, which opens by noting that organised schooling for blind pupils dates only from 1784. Drawing on census figures, it puts the share of blind people at about one in five hundred in Asia. In Africa the share is about one in three hundred. In Europe it is about one in eleven hundred. In all, it reckons near two and a half million blind people alive in the world.

Heat, glare, snow light, and disease help explain why blindness clusters in hot lands and near the poles. The entry then traces teaching methods. These include raised print, the Moon system, and Braille, with its dots read by touch. It surveys schools and workshops country by country, and notes Catholic care for blind pupils. Readers get both the scale of the need and the slow craft of meeting it.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-ermland:
Ermland, or Ermeland, is a district of East Prussia and an exempt bishopric. Saint Adalbert of Prague, dead in 997, and Saint Bruno of Querfurt, dead in 1009, converted the heathen Prussians of this region to Christianity. Two centuries later Teutonic Knights and Cistercians brought civilization into the land as well. In 1243 the possessions of the Teutonic Knights were divided into the dioceses of Culm, Pomesanien, Ermland, and Samland.

Albert of Suerbeer, a Cologne man and former Archbishop of Armagh in Ireland, was appointed Archbishop of Prussia. In 1251 he chose Riga as his see, confirmed by Alexander IV, who in 1255 made Riga metropolitan over the four dioceses. It was not until 28 August 1251 that the first actual bishop was consecrated. Anselm of Meissen, also a Teutonic Knight priest, was consecrated at Valenciennes by the papal legate Pietro of Albano.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-established-c:
The Established Church of Scotland dates from August 1560. In that month the Scottish Parliament decided that the Protestant Confession of Faith should be the established, and only authorized, creed of the kingdom. Papal jurisdiction fell to the same Parliament's abolition, and hearing or celebrating Mass drew a death penalty under its ban. Yet appointing or maintaining the new clergy got no provision from it.

December 1560 brought the first General Assembly, and there the First Book of Discipline won approval. Doctrine, worship, the election of ministers, and their generous support from the confiscated revenues of the ancient Church all fell under its legislation. Ten districts divided Scotland, each with a travelling superintendent who instituted ministers and set the Church in order. A scheme for popular and higher education, much praised, was sketched by the Reformers, but they never carried it out.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-finland:
Finland was then a grand duchy of the Russian Empire, a land of lakes and forests. Its people, about 2,900,000 souls, were chiefly Finns, with Swedish settlers on the coasts. Christianity came from both east and west: Russian missionaries reached Karelia, and Erik of Sweden crusaded in 1157. An independent church order grew under Bishop Thomas, whose see later moved to Åbo.

The last Catholic bishop resigned in 1523, and Gustavus Vasa pressed Lutheranism on the land. By the sixteenth century's end the Catholic Church in Finland had ceased to exist. Under Russian rule from 1809, Catholics regained the right to exist, but numbered only about 1,000 souls. Most Finns belonged to the Lutheran National Church, in four dioceses with 512 parishes.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-francis-patri:
Francis Patrick McFarland, born at Franklin, Pennsylvania, on 16 April 1819 and dead at Hartford, Connecticut, on 2 October 1874, was the third Bishop of Hartford. His parents, John McFarland and Mary McKeever, had emigrated from Armagh, and from childhood he leaned toward the priesthood. After teaching in a village school he entered Mount St. Mary's College, Emmitsburg, graduated with high honours, stayed on as teacher, and was ordained at New York by Archbishop Hughes on 18 May 1845.

Hughes set him to teach at St. John's College, Fordham, but McFarland longed for parish ministry and made missionary journeys among scattered Catholics. After a year he became pastor at Watertown, New York, then in 1851 at St. John's, Utica, where seven years of saintly labour won notice as far as Rome. He declined the vicariate of Florida in 1857, was elected Bishop of Hartford, consecrated at Providence in 1858, and resided there until his diocese was divided in 1872.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-francois-rene:
Francois-Rene de Chateaubriand, born at Saint-Malo in Brittany on 4 September 1768 and dead at Paris on 4 July 1848. He was a French writer whose Genius of Christianity helped restore Catholic imagination after the Revolution.

When the monarchy fell he sailed for America on 8 April 1791, and the wilderness gave his poetic mind inexhaustible imagery. But on Louis XVI's arrest at Varennes he felt duty-bound to serve imperilled royalty, returned to France on 2 January 1792, married, and emigrated.
