He joined Conde's army, was wounded and left for dead before Thionville, and escaped to England in 1793. There he lived in abject misery in London until 1800, returning under an assumed name. His Genius of Christianity, published in 1802, made him famous at once, winning him a Rome embassy secretaryship from Bonaparte and a place in the French Academy.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-free-church-o:
The Free Church of Scotland broke from the established Church in 1843 over who should control the Church's own life. Known since 1900 as the United Free Church, it counted more than half a million of Scotland's Presbyterians by 1908. The entry traces a long fight over patronage, the right of private patrons to name parish ministers.

Scottish Presbyterians had claimed freedom from civil meddling since 1560, but the 1712 act restored private patronage. The Assembly's Veto Act of 1834 let congregations refuse an unwanted presentee, yet civil courts struck it down in the Auchterarder case of 1838. After a Ten Years Conflict, the evangelical party walked out in 1843 rather than yield the Church's spiritual freedom to the state.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-garland:
Garland means a wreath of flowers or evergreens once worn at baptism, weddings, funerals, and solemn processions. The earliest sure baptismal garland comes from seventh-century Alexandria, where the priest crowned the newly baptized after communion. The custom lingered there into the eighteenth century. A Gallican phrase about the baptized and crowned in Christ likely speaks in metaphor instead.

Bridal crowns began with pagan Greeks, passed to Romans, and by Chrysostom's day crowned Christian couples as victors over fleshly temptation. The Greek Church keeps the rite with silver crowns. Funeral wreaths first honored virgin martyrs, then all martyrs, and in England maids' garlands hung above graves into recent times, notably in Devon and Cornwall. Clergy too wore rose garlands in procession.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-george-of-tre:
George of Trebizond, a Greek scholar born in Crete in 1395, carried Greek learning into Renaissance Italy. Named for his family's Trebizond origin, he arrived about 1420, before Constantinople's fall, and swapped lessons with Vittorino da Feltre at Mantua, Latin for Greek. After Venice and Florence he reached Rome, where Eugenius IV gave him a leading professorship at the restored university in 1431.

Nicholas V prized him as a translator of Ptolemy and Eusebius, but arrogance and quarrels with Bessarion, Gaza, and Poggio drove him to Naples. His former pupil Paul II restored him as papal abbreviator, yet fresh quarrels followed. Siding with Aristotle against Plethon's Plato, he lost Bessarion's friendship, whose reply counted 259 errors in his translation of Plato's Laws. He died resenting obscurity in 1486.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-greenland:
Greenland is an island stretching from within the Arctic Circle south to about 59 degrees north latitude, between 20 and 75 degrees west longitude. Roughly triangular with its apex pointing south, it is bounded by the Arctic Ocean, Smith Sound, Baffin's Bay, Davis Strait, and the Atlantic. A Catholic Encyclopedia article follows a land of ice, fiords, and hard winters.

The interior is a plateau rising toward the east, with peaks above 13,100 feet. Immense ice fields launch glaciers to the sea. Only the southwestern valleys and south-facing hills grow vegetation, and farming is out of the question, though lettuce and cabbage thrive comparatively well. Ivigtut, outside Siberia, is the only known source of kryolite, used in making aluminum.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-guitmund:
Norman Benedictine Guitmund, later Bishop of Aversa, defended the doctrine of Transubstantiation against Berengarius of Tours in the eleventh century. A pupil of Lanfranc at Bec alongside St. Anselm, he refused a bishopric from William the Conqueror in 1070 and boldly called the Norman conquest of England robbery.

Between 1073 and 1077 he wrote his dialogue treatise On the Truth of the Body and Blood of Jesus Christ in the Eucharist, answering Berengarius point by point. His account of how Christ is present stays unclear, and he treats the decay of the species as a trick of the senses. Taking the name Christianus in Rome, he was made Bishop of Aversa by Urban II in 1088 and died there between 1090 and 1095.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-helinand:
Flemish-born poet and chronicler Hélinand, born at Pronleroi about 1150, won Philip Augustus's favour as a worldly courtier before turning Cistercian at Froidmont about 1190 and becoming a model of piety. Whatever hours monastic duty left, he gave to study, preaching after ordination, and writing, and Beauvais honours him as a saint on 3 February.

Surviving works fill a large stretch of Migne. There are twenty-eight sermons in neat Latin steeped in pagan poets and Fathers, two ascetic treatises, a letter recalling a renegade monk, and a passion of Theban Legion martyrs. A world chronicle to 1204 follows, its early part lost and its history too uncritical for much weight. A French poem on death survives in only four broken stanzas.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-henry-harland:
Henry Harland, a novelist born at St. Petersburg in 1861 to New England parents, studied theology briefly at Harvard and spent a year in Italy, returning a Catholic at heart. Rising at four before his day's work at the Surrogate's Court, he wrote As It Was Written and a Jewish trilogy signed Sidney Luska, a name he later wished forgotten. In London from 1887 he wrote stories collected in Mademoiselle Miss, Grey Roses, and Comedies and Errors.

Harland founded The Yellow Book in 1894 with Aubrey Beardsley. It made both men lions of the hour until failing health ended it in 1897, the year he and his wife entered the Church. His later novels, The Cardinal's Snuff Box, The Lady Paramount, and My Friend Prospero, are pervaded by Catholic faith. A physician gave him two years at thirty; he lived fourteen fruitful ones, dying at San Remo in 1905.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-henry-ii-king:
Henry II, king of England from 1154, was born in 1133 to Matilda, daughter of Henry I, and Geoffrey Plantagenet, from whom he inherited Anjou, Touraine, and Maine. Knighted at sixteen, ruler of Normandy and Anjou at eighteen, husband of Eleanor of Aquitaine at nineteen, he forced Stephen to terms at twenty and took the crown a year later. With his chancellor Thomas Becket he crushed feudal resistance, surrendered castles, and reorganized the exchequer and royal justice, reforms later embodied in the Assizes.

Prosperity broke on his quarrel with Becket, raised to Canterbury in 1162. Henry's attack on the jurisdiction of church courts produced the Constitutions of Clarendon, six years of persecution. Becket's murder in 1170, followed by Henry's barefoot penance at the martyr's shrine in 1174. The rebellions of his sons, probably stirred by Eleanor, embittered his closing years. He died on 6 July 1189, a king whose legal reforms outlasted his personal tragedies.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-hucbald-of-st:
Hucbald of St. Amand was a Benedictine monk, born in 840 and dead in 930 or 932, whose birthplace is unknown. He entered the order at St. Amand near Tournai and added music to his studies, then completed his general and artistic education at St. Germain d'Auxerre. By 883 he taught at St. Bertin, and with Rémi d'Auxerre he restored the old church singing schools in the diocese of Reims in 892.

Hucbald worked to improve neumatic notation, which showed melody's rhythm but left intervals to tradition. After trying Greek notation again, he invented the Dazia signs, which mark intervals and church modes plainly. Those signs proved clumsy and never won lasting favour, so he later fixed the scale's intervals with lines and the Latin alphabet's first letters, a step toward modern notation.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-iceland:
Iceland is a North Atlantic island, counted with Europe by population and history though really part of America. It lies between set northern latitudes, separated from the New World by the ice-bound Strait of Greenland. Much indented by fjords on northern and western shores, it covers about forty thousand square miles, only two-fifths of it habitable.

From a barren, rocky plateau averaging two thousand feet high rise glaciers, broad summits, and volcanic mountains such as Hecla and Oeraefa. Those peaks have belched lava and mud to great havoc in eruptions like those of 1783, 1845, and 1873. Earthquakes are frequent, rivers short but full, and inland lakes many. The climate is oceanic, with moderate temperature swings and frequent fogs, and the entry goes on to Iceland's people, history, and church.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-ireland:
Ireland, set in the Atlantic west of Great Britain, is surveyed here on the encyclopedia's largest scale, from its coasts to its saints. At most it is 302 miles long and 174 miles wide. It covers 32,535 square miles in four provinces and thirty-two counties. Its center is a level plain ringed by coastal mountains. Many rivers and bays cut it. Its climate is mild yet very moist. Its soil suits farming and pasture better than mining.

Ancient names — Ierna, Juverna, Hibernia, Ogygia, Inisfail — open a history that runs through early kings, missionaries, Norse raids, Norman conquest, and later centuries of penal law and revival. Geography, peoples, church organization, schools, and literature each get their section. Readers find a whole country in one entry, written just before the political upheavals that would soon reshape it.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-jacques-sirmo:
Scholar Jacques Sirmond ranked among the greatest of the seventeenth century. He was born at Riom in Puy-de-Dôme in October 1559. He died at Paris on 7 October 1651. He entered the Society of Jesus in 1576. In 1581 he became professor of classical languages at Paris. There he counted St Francis de Sales among his pupils. Called to Rome in 1590, he served sixteen years as private secretary to Superior General Aquaviva.

During those years he spent leisure moments studying antiquity's literary and historical treasures. He kept close ties with learned men then at Rome, including Bellarmine and Baronius. He helped Baronius compose the Annales. In 1608 he returned to Paris. In 1637 he became confessor to King Louis XIII. His first literary work appeared in 1610. From then until life's end, almost every year saw a new publication. The entry presents a Jesuit antiquarian at Europe's scholarly center.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-jean-allemand: Jean Allemand, a French priest and scholar of Eastern languages born in 1799 and dead in 1833. He taught Scripture at the Roman Seminary and served as a consultor and censor in Rome. He also edited a journal of religious science. His known writings defend purgatory against an English critic and warn against Champollion's reading of Egyptian hieroglyphs.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-jean-baptiste:
Jean-Baptiste-Antoine Ferland, a French-Canadian historian born at Montreal in 1805 and dead at Quebec in 1865, spent his youth gathering notes on Canada's past before he ever wrote a book. Ordained in 1828, he served country parishes, then directed studies and later led the college of Nicolet.

Ferland turned to print only near forty, answering a rival church history in 1853 and publishing notes on Quebec parish registers. Named professor of Canadian history at Laval in 1855, he gathered fresh papers in France and drew large crowds to his public lectures from 1858 to 1862. Those lectures, printed as his Course of Canadian History, fixed his name as a founder of the field.

Jean-Baptiste Marchand, a Sulpician priest born at Verchères in 1760 and dead at Sandwich, Ontario, in 1825. He led Montreal College and then served the Hurons at Detroit for nearly thirty years. Ordained in 1786, he joined the Montreal Sulpicians in 1788. He soon headed their college, then Saint Raphael's.

In 1796 Marchand succeeded to the Huron mission at Assumption parish opposite Detroit, now Sandwich. A bishop's first recorded visit there in 1801 confirmed some five hundred people, and an assistant came, though he was recalled in 1806. Marchand laboured on mostly alone, tending a frontier flock through war, change, and distance from Quebec.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-jocelin-de-br:
Jocelin de Brakelond, a late-twelfth-century English chronicler, was the Bury Saint Edmunds monk. His abbey history under feeble Abbot Hugh and energetic Abbot Sampson gave Carlyle material for the second book of Past and Present. Entering the abbey in 1173, Jocelin learned under novice-master Sampson, who made him chaplain and constant companion when he became abbot in 1182.

Jocelin served as chaplain to 1188, guest-master a decade later, and almoner in 1212, last heard in April 1215 advising Abbot Hugh II on manors. His chronicle runs from 1173 to 1202, including Henry of Essex's tale, and was first edited for the Camden Society in 1843, the edition Carlyle used. Shrewd, kindly, and plainly truthful, Jocelin won Carlyle's warm praise.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-john-almond:
John Almond was a Cistercian monk counted among the confessors of the faith under Elizabeth I. A native of Cheshire, he had been a monk in Henry VIII's reign. The name of his abbey is not known. His fate during and after the suppression of the monasteries cannot be traced.

His closing sufferings are known from an account printed by Foley. It tells of an aged priest worn down by imprisonment, left in Hull Castle to pine away under revolting neglect until his death on 18 April 1585. The supplementary process of the English martyrs included his case. It stands as a stark example of what Elizabethan prisons did to Catholic priests who would not conform.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-john-england:
John England was the first Bishop of Charleston and a leading voice for Catholic emancipation in Ireland and America. Born at Cork in 1786, he entered Carlow College in 1803 and preached to crowded congregations. He founded poor schools from which the Presentation Convent grew, and was ordained in 1809. His pen and tongue assailed the Veto measure of 1814, and next to O'Connell his influence was greatest in the agitation for emancipation.

Consecrated Bishop of Charleston at Cork in 1820, he refused the customary oath of allegiance to Britain. He reached Charleston that December to find a diocese of three states with Catholics scattered in little groups. He built up churches, schools, and a seminary, and edited a diocesan paper. He defended the Church in public controversy until his death at Charleston in 1842, leaving a model of an American bishop in a missionary age.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-john-garland:
John Garland was an English poet and grammarian who spent most of his life teaching in France. Born in England, he studied at Oxford under John of London, one of Roger Bacon's masters, then was fostered in France, a land he cherished above his birthplace. He studied at Paris, and grammar and belles-lettres were his subjects at Toulouse and later at Paris.

Reaching Toulouse near the close of the Albigensian war, he wrote about 1229 an epithalamium for the Virgin. He also wrote his epic On the Triumphs of the Church, celebrating crusading victories and the crushing of heresy. Back in Paris by 1234, he composed a poem on accent in over fourteen hundred hexameters and a poem on the liturgy. He also wrote schoolbooks in verse: glossaries, a grammar compendium, lists of homonyms, a rhetoric, and a collection of versification examples. He took his name from Paris's Rue Garlande.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-joseph-olivie:
Joseph Olivier Briand was the seventh Bishop of Quebec and a second founder of Canada's Church. Born at Plérin in Brittany in 1715 and ordained in 1739, he secretly left home to follow Bishop Pontbriand to Canada. As vicar-general he ran the diocese during the siege of Quebec in 1759 and tended the dying at Ste-Foy in 1760.

After the British conquest, Briand judged that allegiance must change and worked to secure the Church under London. Consecrated at Paris in 1766, he won the Quebec Act of 1774, which let Catholics hold public office and confirmed religious freedom. He declined clergy gifts for his support and lived at the Quebec Seminary.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-kaiserwilhelm:
Kaiserwilhelmsland was the German portion of the island of New Guinea, some 460,000 square miles with about a million inhabitants. The first Catholic missionaries arrived in August 1896, three priests and three brothers, and twelve stations soon lined a coast some four hundred miles long. The little mission steamer Gabriel linked them. An apostolic prefecture set up in 1896 passed to the Society of the Divine Word.

By 1909 the mission counted twenty-two priests, seventeen lay brothers, and twenty-nine sisters, though no native priests yet, and a cathedral, St. Michael's at Alexishafen, was already planned. Thirteen parochial schools taught six hundred pupils, and some 1,960 baptisms had taken place since the start. Language was the great difficulty: about 120 pupils at St. Michael's spoke twenty-five different tongues. Adults also learned trades like carpentry, smith-work, boat-building, and tailoring, in hopes the mission might one day support itself.

Charles Kingsley wrote this essay in defence of Froude's History of England, and the hosted text comes from the 1890 edition of his Plays and Puritans and Other Historical Essays. He begins with a provocation: a recent Comic History of England, all caricature, struck thoughtful readers as a crime. Then, he says, they reflected that the comic book only carried to its height the method of a hundred years of English history-writing.

Kingsley's charge is that modern historians treat the past as a pageant of fools and knaves, solved in advance by Gibbon and Voltaire. Against that school he sets Froude, whose history honours its subject and trusts its characters. The essay is part review, part sermon on reverence in history. Kingsley the novelist and clergyman argues that laughter at our forefathers is a failure of imagination, not a proof of enlightenment.
getting-gold-a-practical-treatise-for-pr:
J. C. F. Johnson, an Australian mining engineer, wrote Getting Gold as a working manual. Charles Griffin published the revised second edition in London in 1898. Johnson had sold ten thousand copies of his earlier Practical Mining, mostly in Australasia. Gold fever, he knew, sends green men into the field with more hope than skill.

Chapters cover finding gold-bearing ground, washing river sands, and breaking quartz from the lode. Mill work, ore treatment, and the handling of gold after it leaves the ground get plain directions. Two closing chapters of rules of thumb pack hints for prospectors, mill operators, managers, and company directors. Johnson mixes his own field discoveries with picked advice from other miners. Students of mining history read the book for its period methods, costs, and slang. Prospectors of its day read it for survival: how to test a claim before hunger and debt tested them.
govdocs-archive_org-nsia-BirminghamIndic: Birmingham Indictment (Fragment): the fragment of a federal indictment from Birmingham citing 18 USC. section 341 - the garbled OCR obscures the rest. A damaged capture, kept as found. A legal fragment. From the archive shelves, for readers.
govdocs-archive_org-nsia-BlavatskyFounda: nsia-BlavatskyFoundation Blavatsky Foundation: the made public government document on the Blavatsky Foundation, captured as titled. Subject: government records. A bare file, kept as issued. An obscure item, of the files. From the archive shelves, for readers.
govdocs-archive_org-nsia-CIAEngland_CIA_:
Christopher Walker's article reports a delicate matter: CIA men working in Britain, checking on subversion on the territory of America's closest ally. Stories of that kind tested the special relationship whenever they surfaced in print.

The piece belongs to the 1970s wave of reporting on the agency's reach into friendly countries, when the British press took a hard look at American intelligence activity in London. What the officers were watching, and with whose permission, were the questions such reporting pressed. The single article is preserved among the archive's clippings on the CIA abroad.
govdocs-archive_org-nsia-PublicityEnglan: Robert Pitman wrote for the Sunday Express, a British newspaper, an article headlined 'What is the TRUTH about...' The headline is cut off in the scan, so the article's promised truth cannot be named. The file keeps the piece under a publicity heading for the Oswald case, which suggests its theme. Beyond the author, the paper, and the partial headline, the evidence here preserves nothing of the article's contents.
govdocs-nsarchive-Briefing_Book_cuba-rus:
Anastas Mikoyan survived at the top of Soviet politics from Stalin through Khrushchev, a rare feat. Svetlana Savranskaya edited this briefing book, number 735, published in December 2020. Russian archival records marked 125 years since the revolutionary-turned-statesman's birth.

The records catch Mikoyan in unusual moments. In 1936 he told the Soviet Central Committee that they needed to learn from America. He held secret talks with Fidel Castro, with Shah Reza Pahlavi of Iran, and with Dwight Eisenhower. The portrait is of a smiling diplomat sent in first whenever Moscow faced a delicate problem.
govdocs-nsarchive-Briefing_Book_iran_US-: Forty years of US-Iran bad blood: antagonism, distrust, and fear in this National Security Archive briefing-book capture. The made-public record of a long feud. A single capture, dated. From the archive set.
govdocs-nsarchive-Briefing_Book_mexico-a:
Eleven years after forty-three Ayotzinapa students were forcibly disappeared in Mexico, Kate Doyle and Claire Dorfman edited this briefing book, posted in September 2025. Its subject is the role of the United States Drug Enforcement Administration in the case's long story. The anniversary, it says, brings a grim reckoning.

Evidence here gives the editors, date, and agency focus, and little more. Even so, the angle matters: American drug enforcement worked closely with Mexican security forces in that era. What the DEA knew, shared, or withheld belongs in any full account of a crime that Mexico's own investigations have struggled to settle.
govdocs-nsarchive-Briefing_Book_mexico_E:
Luis Echeverría, president of Mexico in the early 1970s, managed dissent with a strategy officials called co-opt and control. This Archive posting reviews his legacy in that system. It draws on a CIA assessment of his responsibility for a defining atrocity of the period.

The CIA judged that Echeverría shares heavily in the blame for the Tlatelolco massacre, in which government forces killed student protesters in 1968, before his presidency. Co-opting critics with jobs and favors, while controlling the rest, shaped Mexican politics for years. The posting weighs that machinery against the violence it rested on.
govdocs-nsarchive-Briefing_Book_nuclear-:
Nuclear alerts and raised readiness levels, the DEFCONs, mark the moments the Cold War came closest to firing. William Burr edited this briefing book, updated in May 2021. Its headline item is a top-secret 1966 RAND summary report posted publicly for the first time.

That report concluded the United States came fairly close to using tactical nuclear weapons during the Taiwan Strait Crisis of 1958. A finding like that, written by analysts close to the events, carries weight. The set lets readers trace how alerts worked in practice: who raised them, how far they went, and how they were stood down.

New Declassifications on Nuclear Weapons Safety and Security: the National Security Archive briefing-book page capture. The archivists capture, complete. A single capture. Dated material. From the archive's collection, for researchers of the records and readers.
govdocs-nsarchive-Briefing_Book_nunn-lug:
Ukraine inherited part of the Soviet nuclear arsenal when the Soviet Union collapsed, then gave the weapons up. This Archive posting traces that story to a closing image. At Pervomaysk, where an ICBM silo once stood, officials held a sunflower-planting ceremony in 1996.

Sunflowers were chosen to root in the soil of a missile field and to symbolize a future without the weapons. The posting pairs the arsenal's scale with the ceremony's smallness: seeds in a silo field. For readers, the record preserves the disarmament end of the Ukraine story, the part that later wars have pushed out of memory.
govdocs-nsarchive-Briefing_Book_russia-p:
Vladimir Putin was the first foreign leader to call President George W. Bush after the attacks of September 11, 2001. National Security Archive Briefing Book number 914 publishes transcripts of their talks. Edited by Svetlana Savranskaya and Tom Blanton, it traces how the two men built a working bond around the fight against terrorism.

The records quote Putin calling the United States invaluable on Afghanistan and using blunt language about destroying shared enemies. Bush answers in kind. Yet the transcripts also show Putin opposing the American invasion of Iraq, warning that force must not replace law between nations. Together the talks chart a partnership that was real, warm at the top, and still limited by clashing interests.
govdocs-nsarchive-News_cyber-vault_Cyber:
American election security became a pressing worry after the 2016 vote, when foreign interference and hacking fears put state systems under a spotlight. A National Security Archive cyber brief, edited by Michael Martelle, gathers the plans and stated priorities of the states themselves, setting out how each one meant to protect its elections.

State-by-state detail is the value here. Voting in the United States is run locally, so defenses, budgets, and weak points differ sharply from one capital to the next. A side-by-side record lets readers compare promises with practice and see which risks officials took seriously. For anyone tracing how election protection grew from an afterthought into a standing duty, the brief is a useful snapshot of the states' own words.
govdocs-nsarchive-News_cyber-vault_Sting:
Police in the United States use devices called stingrays to track cell phones, often in secret. A National Security Archive news post from November 2019 covers these tools, also known as IMSI-catchers. They work by pretending to be a cell tower, so nearby phones connect to them and reveal their identity.

The secrecy is the story. For years, departments bought stingrays under agreements that kept even judges and defense lawyers from learning how the tracking worked or how often it swept up innocent people's phones. A short brief like this one gives readers the basic facts of the technology and the legal fight around it. It is a starting point for understanding a surveillance tool most people have never seen, though many have passed within its range.
govdocs-nsarchive-News_foia_Trump_Visito: The fight over Donald Trump's White House visitor logs reached the Second Circuit. That is the federal appeals court in New York. A National Security Archive briefing book page follows the case there. The Archive and its partners argued the public has a right to know who visits the president; the government argued the logs are presidential records beyond the disclosure law's reach. Only the page capture survives here, marking one stop in a suit testing how far transparency law follows a president's guests.
hebbel-mutter-und-kind:
A mother's love, in joy and in terror, carries Hebbel's epic poem Mutter und Kind, given here in German. Mother and Child follows the bond from first delight through trials that test it to the edge. Hebbel wrote in powerful, somber verse quite unlike his stage works, yet unmistakably his.

Everyday devotion reveals tragic depths under his gaze, as it does throughout his writing. The poem moves through the seasons of a child's growth and a mother's fears. Less known than the plays, it shares their weight and moral seriousness. Readers who meet Hebbel first as a dramatist will find a different music here. The poem also shows the nineteenth century learning to treat motherhood as an epic subject.
held-fast-for-england: Held Fast for England, G, a, henty's peninsular tale, the steadfast. This book preserves that historical novel. The archive guards it with care. Those who study the era will use it. The archive keeps the paper open to all.
herland: Gilman's 1915 Herland imagines an all-female utopia found by explorers. Men gape. The Tower library holds the full text. It dreamed women-only. Explorers came. Mothers ruled. Utopia challenged. More detail helps readers grasp the key points well. More detail helps readers grasp the key points well. More detail helps readers grasp the key points well.
heroic-romances-of-ireland-translated-in:
Heroic Romances of Ireland, translated into English prose and verse by A H Leahy, presents the oldest Irish tales in Volume 1 of two. Leahy opens with a preface arguing that Ireland's early literature deserves the attention Greek and Roman classics receive, though it comes from a world even stranger to modern readers. Special introductions and notes frame each romance for newcomers.

The volume centers on the great cattle raid story, the Tain bo Cuailnge, in the version from the Book of Leinster, with two versions compared. Around it stand shorter heroic tales of kings, warriors, and the deeds that made their names. Leahy renders the Irish into both verse and plain prose, so readers can feel the poetry and still follow the plot. Warriors like Cuchulain move through a pagan Ireland of forts, cattle wealth, and single combat.
history-of-king-charles-the-second-of-en:
Jacob Abbott's History of King Charles the Second of England retells the Restoration king's life for young readers, as part of Abbott's history series. Abbott promises strict truth rather than tales founded on history, saying that even minute details rest on what he judged good historical authority from the annals of the time.

The narrative follows Charles from exile through his return to the throne and his reign, keeping embellishment out and letting events speak. Abbott admits that all histories carry some imperfection and error, but insists that nothing here is stated without a source he trusted. The book suits younger readers meeting Stuart England for the first time, and older readers curious about how nineteenth-century America taught its children history.
history-of-the-warfare-of-science-with-t:
Andrew Dickson White, cofounder and first president of Cornell, published his History of the Warfare of Science with Theology in Christendom in two volumes, here combined. He dedicates the book to Ezra Cornell and argues that dogmatic theology repeatedly blocked inquiry, while true religion and science need not fight. The first volume runs from creation to evolution.

White marshals centuries of cases: astronomy, geology, medicine, and biblical criticism, each traced from ancient views through church resistance to modern conclusions. The middle chapters weigh how theologians debated even the form God took at the Redemption. His learning is vast and his side clear. The book remains a founding text of the conflict thesis historians still argue about.
holberg-niels-klim-s-journey-under-the-g:
Niels Klim falls through a cave mouth and finds a whole world under the ground in Holberg's novel, here in English. Strange peoples live there, and walking, talking trees hold reason in high esteem. Holberg first published the tale in Latin in 1741.

Klim's tour of odd kingdoms lets Holberg mock pride, greed, and folly back home. Each land twists one human habit until its absurd side shows clearly. The book works as both wild invention and sharp satire. Often likened to Gulliver's Travels, it gave Scandinavia a classic of wit that still reads fresh and strange.
how-he-lied-to-her-husband:
George Bernard Shaw wrote How He Lied to Her Husband in four rainy days in Scotland in 1905, as a curtain-raiser for actor Arnold Daly in New York. Shaw's preface calls the husband, wife, and lover triangle the stalest situation on stage. He claims fresh treatment can save it. His lovers meet over a packet of lost poems.

Aurora Bompas has lost the love poems Henry Apjohn wrote to her. Every poem names her, and Aurora is, she protests, the only Aurora in London. Discovery would ruin her marriage and her name. Henry refuses to be sensible about the danger. When the husband confronts them, Henry's lying takes an unexpected direction. Shaw turns farce machinery into a small study of vanity and honor. Readers get a one-act comedy that mocks romantic convention while using it expertly.
how-sammy-went-to-coral-land:
Emily Paret Atwater's How Sammy Went to Coral-Land is a children's story that mingles fiction with natural history. Atwater thanks Cooke's Toilers of the Sea and Hartwig's Denizens of the Deep for much of the natural history, trusting young readers to tell fact from fancy.

Sammy goes out to see the world, escapes from a shark, meets a hermit-crab, and encounters star-fish, unsociable oysters and a pilot-fish on his way to coral-land. Illustrations show the hammerheaded shark, the sword-fish, the remora and the torpedo-fish. Children curious about sea life will find Sammy's voyage both instructive and delightful.
how-spring-came-in-new-england:
Charles Dudley Warner's sketch of the New England spring is a comic essay on climate as character. New England, he writes, is the battleground of the seasons, a camp invaded in turn by the legions of the pole and the sirens of the tropics. The compromise between them is called thaw, and thaw is the normal condition.

Warner personifies the weather shamelessly. The Gulf Stream should rescue the region but mostly does not; it is shunted off, too shallow, and mocked by icebergs and Newfoundland fogs. Potatoes ripen in Ireland before they are planted in New England. Yet the climate makes the man, he argues: a New-Englander, always just about to be warm, is the stuff of heroes and martyrs. It is one short essay, built like a stand-up routine a century early.
howards-end:
E. M. Forster builds this novel around a small Hertfordshire house and the two families who contend for it. It opens with Helen Schlegel's letters to her sister Margaret from Howards End, where she is visiting the Wilcox family. The house is old red brick under a great wych-elm, and Helen reports that Mrs. Wilcox loves it as no one else does.

Forster sets the Schlegel sisters, raised on books, music, and talk, against the Wilcox men of business and motor cars. A mistaken engagement, a clerk named Leonard Bast with his umbrella and his Ruskin, and a deathbed note about the house bind the families together. Margaret's marriage into the Wilcox world tests the novel's famous command to connect. The country house becomes the measure of England itself: who shall inherit it, and on what terms.
it-is-never-too-late-to-mend:
Charles Reade's It Is Never Too Late to Mend opens on a failing Berkshire farm. George Fielding works The Grove, four hundred acres of poor sour land, with his brother William. Frank Winchester, a gay and original gentleman, rides into his troubles. Fielding is sober, proud, intelligent, and desperately unlucky.

Love for Susan Merton drives Fielding to desperate borrowing, and suspicion of theft destroys him. Reade follows him into prison, where a cruel governor and a kind chaplain fight for his soul. A reformed thief's story interweaves with the farmer's fall. The Australian goldfields offer the ruined men a second world. The novel made Reade famous as an exposé of prison discipline. Its title is its gospel: no man, however broken, is past mending.
john-bull-s-other-island:
John Bull's Other Island is a play by Bernard Shaw about England and Ireland. It opens at Great George Street, Westminster, in the rooms of Doyle and Broadbent, civil engineers. The partners are bachelors and bosom friends who live where they work. Their sitting room smells of tobacco and holds drawing boards, plans, and tracing paper.

On the walls hang a map of South America, a portrait of Gladstone, and cartoons of Balfour and Chamberlain. The time is a summer afternoon in 1904, as the scene directions fix it. Broadbent, the English partner, arrives with luggage in the first moments. Doyle, his Irish partner, gives Shaw his pair for the argument ahead: English confidence meets Irish clear sight in business and politics.
landholding-in-england:
Joseph Fisher wrote this history of landholding in England. He signed himself a fellow of the Royal Historical Society. A proverb about tillage and judgment stands as his motto.

Fisher argues that farming is the most useful of all arts. A nation draws its food and solid wealth from the soil, he says. His history traces how English land was held across the ages. Laws, customs, and great estates all shape that story. The book suits readers curious about how land law grew in England. Fisher links land law to the daily bread of the poor. That link gives dry legal history a human stake.
letters-of-a-traveller-or-notes-of-thing:
William Cullen Bryant gathered his Letters of a Traveller from sixteen years of journeys. The letters record things seen in Europe and America. Bryant admits they form no regular account of any single tour.

Instead, he offers occasional sketches of whatever caught his attention. Most pieces had already appeared in print before this collection. Bryant, a poet and newspaper editor, writes with a traveler's calm curiosity. Scenery, towns, and customs all receive his measured attention. The book preserves an early American voice observing the wider world. Bryant helped found the New York Evening Post's voice. Travel gave his editorials a wider, calmer horizon.
letters-of-franz-liszt-volume-2-from-rom: "From Rome to the End" is the subtitle of this second volume of Franz Liszt's correspondence. It takes up where the Paris-to-Rome volume leaves off, in the composer's later years. The editor was La Mara, and Constance Bache translated the letters into English. Because the hosted sample holds nothing past the Project Gutenberg header, no contents are described here; the title page is the whole evidence.
lewis-rand:
Mary Johnston published her novel Lewis Rand in 1908. Houghton Mifflin issued it at Boston and New York, with pictures by F. C. Yohn. Johnston had written To Have and to Hold and Prisoners of Hope.

She inscribed the book to Senator John Tyler Morgan's memory. Thirty years a senator, he was a good man and patriot, she writes. Her tale turns to Virginia politics in Jefferson's era. Ambition drives the hero whose name titles the book. Courtship and courtrooms, one picture caption jokes, both await him. Johnston's Virginia settings drew on deep family roots there. Aaron Burr's era shadows the politics behind her romance.
life-in-morocco-and-glimpses-beyond:
Budgett Meakin wrote this account of life in Morocco. His earlier books described the Moors and the land itself. Contents range across dress, courtesy, food, slavery, and trade. Festivals, saints, marriage, and funeral rites all receive chapters.

Meakin also treats the Berbers and the Jews of Morocco. City descriptions run from Tangier and Fez to far southern towns. Travel pieces recall journeys in Moorish guise and by bicycle. The volume offers a full, close portrait of Moroccan society. His Land of the Moors described towns from Tangier to Mogador. Reminiscences include a bicycle journey to Marrákesh and Moorish disguise.
life-of-harriet-beecher-stowe-compiled-f:
Charles Edward Stowe compiled this life of his mother from her papers. Houghton, Mifflin published it in Boston and New York in 1890. Harriet Beecher Stowe suggested the compilation herself, her son explains. Failing strength kept her from writing the recollections alone.

With her limited assistance, he built the story from letters and journals. The preface carries her own notes of instruction for readers. A handwritten letter appears among the illustrations. The result lets the author of Uncle Tom's Cabin speak largely for herself. The Riverside Press at Cambridge printed the electrotyped sheets. A Richmond portrait of Stowe fronts the compiled letters.
lonesome-land:
B. M. Bower opens this western novel with Val's arrival. Well-meant advice and a lady in a temper follow quickly. A shivaree and Cold Spring Ranch set the scene. Manley's fire guard and a prairie fire raise the stakes.

Kent rides to the rescue after desolation strikes the ranch. Val's awakening leads her toward becoming an author. A blotched brand and Kent's confession complicate the middle. Bower had written Chip, of the Flying U, before this tale. Val decides and Kent confesses before the compact chapter. Retribution closes the twenty-four chapter contents list.
maiwa-s-revenge-or-the-war-of-the-little:
Maiwa's Revenge, or The War of the Little Hand, is an Allan Quatermain tale by H. Rider Haggard. Quatermain tells it a week after his story of the Three Lions. The preface swears its strangest incident was 'plagiarized' from real life. Chief Mandara, on Africa's east coast, truly owned the 'thing that bites.'

Eight short chapters carry the tale from Gobo's blow to Maiwa avenged. A morning's sport turns into rounds of real fighting. Maiwa's message brings a plan of campaign and an attack. Wambe, her cruel husband, has wronged her past pardon. Haggard writes swift, red-blooded African adventure. The story shows Quatermain in a short, sharp war.
malayan-literature-comprising-romantic-t:
Malayan Literature gathers romantic tales, epic poetry, and royal chronicles in English. Chauncey C. Starkweather translated them, he says, for the first time. His special introduction praises the Epic of Bidasari above all. He calls it the most charming poem of Malayan letters.

Bidasari leads readers through haunted palaces and beauteous gardens. Bowmen and lancers hurry past, then djinns and spirit-princes appear. Starkweather finds imagery and luxury in the old Malay tales. Royal chronicles add kings and courts to the romance. The collection opened a rich, little-known tradition to English readers. It remains a pioneering window onto Southeast Asian letters.
marjorie-s-new-friend:
Marjorie's New Friend is a girls' novel by Carolyn Wells of Patty fame. It opens with a bothersome bag and a welcome Christmas gift. Merry Christmas and Happy New Year carry Marjorie into winter. Then comes a tearful time, with the going of Gladys.

Against that loss stands the coming of Delight, the new friend. A visit to Cinderella, a straw-ride, and making valentines follow. Marjorie is held captive in one chapter and freed in fun. Goldfish, kittens, and a pleasant school fill her days. A sea trip and a valentine party close the year. Wells writes friendship as a child's great adventure.
midwinter-certain-travellers-in-old-engl:
John Buchan published this historical novel in 1923. Its scene is England in 1745, as Bonnie Prince Charlie's rebel army marches south. Alastair Maclean, among the Prince's most loyal supporters, rides ahead on a secret mission. The publisher's description calls the book certain travellers in old England.

On the road Maclean is befriended by two extraordinary men. One is Dr. Samuel Johnson, then an aspiring man of letters. The other is the shadowy figure known only as Midwinter. Buchan blends Jacobite adventure with the talk and travel of Georgian England. The result mixes spying, loyalty, and literary portraiture.
money-island:
Andrew J. Howell Jr. copyrighted this North Carolina story collection in 1908. It was printed at Wilmington by the Commercial Printing Company. The volume holds two tales: Money Island and The Conquest of Jamesby. An illustration shows the little island among the marshes.

Money Island lies in Greenville Sound, not far from Wilmington. The story concerns buried treasure hidden there long ago. Jonathan Landstone told the tale, and wrote it down himself so it would be told correctly. Howell presents the words as Landstone's own. Local legend, a secretive island, and old Carolina families give the tales their flavor of regional history.
multatuli-walter-pieterse-a-story-of-hol:
Multatuli, the pen name of Eduard Douwes Dekker, tells a Dutch boy's growth in Walter Pieterse, here in English. Young Walter, shy and dreamy, comes of age in Amsterdam. His tender heart clashes with a stiff, narrow world of school, church, and trade.

Dekker writes with the satirical fire that made Max Havelaar famous. Here the target is Holland itself: its cant, greed, and small pieties. Walter's first loves and shames carry the author's own boyhood within them. The novel stands as a humane, rebellious classic of Dutch letters, tender toward the young and merciless toward humbug.
my-discovery-of-england:
Stephen Leacock, the Canadian humorist, lectures on his first trip to England. Sir Owen Seaman introduced his first London talk with jokes. Seaman notes Leacock teaches political economy for a living. Humor, he says, is the professor's recreation.

The book grew from those lectures, issued in 1922. Leacock views old England with a colonial's fresh eye. Customs, class, and speech all draw his gentle mockery. V1 praised the tour as sharp yet warm throughout. Leacock never sneers, and his fun cuts both ways. It remains a model of kind satire, proof that a visitor can love a place and laugh at it too.
narratives-of-shipwrecks-of-the-royal-na:
William O. S. Gilly compiled these Royal Navy wreck tales from Admiralty papers. John W. Parker issued the book in London in 1850. His father, Canon William Stephen Gilly, wrote the preface. The wrecks span the war years from 1793 to 1849.

The contents list lost ships in a grim roll call. Boyne, Amphion, Tribune, and Queen Charlotte lead the list. Apollo, Hindostan, Romney, and Venerable follow among many more. Each tale draws on official documents of the loss. Storms, reefs, fire, and war took these ships and crews. The book is a sober memorial to naval disaster in the age of sail.
nasa-tm-19640017347-adaptive-flight-cont:
Lawrence W. Taylor, Jr. and Elmor J. Adkins of NASA's Flight Research Center wrote this paper. They gave it at an AIAA specialists meeting on April 28, 1964. Their subject is adaptive flight control, weighed pro and con. Such systems adjust their own settings while in flight.

The authors say interest grew from trouble with fixed-gain controls. Fast aircraft change character so much that one setting fails. Gain scheduling had fallen from favor for three stated reasons. It needed vast flight data, took long to tune, and broke with each design change. An adaptive system would pick its best gain on its own. The paper weighs that promise for craft like the X-15.
nasa-tm-19650014317-low-speed-investigat:
William P Henderson and Alexander D Hammond at Langley studied a half-wing model that could change its sweep. The pivot sat outboard, away from the body. Their low-speed tests focused on high-lift devices and on sideways control. Leading edge and trailing edge flaps were moved to see their effect.

A swing wing must still take off and land well. At low speed, flaps do much of that work. The tests show how flap settings changed lift and lateral control for this layout. Designers of variable-sweep aircraft needed exactly that kind of data. The half-wing, or semispan, model let them test one side in detail.
nasa-tm-19660006537-saturn-s-i-10-static:
Marshall's Measuring and Evaluation Section issued this final report on January 11, 1966, with vibration and sound data from static tests of Saturn vehicle S-I-10. In a static test, the stage is held down while its engines fire. Sensors record how the vehicle shakes and how loud it becomes. Both can damage the vehicle or its payload if they run too high.

Data appear as acceleration against frequency and sound pressure level against frequency. Statistical profiles complete the record. Engineers use such profiles to set the shaking and noise levels that parts must survive. The report preserves the measured environment of a real Saturn first stage under full thrust.
nasa-tm-19660006764-significant-electron:
Members of the Echo II project staff at Goddard presented this review in San Francisco in August 1965. Project Echo flew giant balloon satellites that bounced signals between ground stations. The review gathers the project's electronic work and its experimental results in one place. Early contents cover the project's objectives and how they were carried out, in a piece by H L Eaker.

Other sections, per the catalog note, treat prototype ground spheres and a television and beacon telemetry system. Communication experiments with Echo II close the set. As a project record, it shows how much ground electronics a supposedly simple balloon satellite actually required to work.
nasa-tm-19660015346-magnetic-field-restr:
Norman F Ness at Goddard wrote rules in July 1964 for keeping stray magnetism out of two spacecraft, IMP-F and IMP-G. The IMP satellites measured magnetic fields in space. A spacecraft's own parts can fake a field and spoil those readings. Ness sets fabrication procedures to prevent that fault. His contents start with non-magnetic electronic and structural parts.

Wiring gets detailed attention, with leads dressed so their fields cancel out. Solar cell wiring and power leads receive their own guidance, as strong stray sources. Magnetic field tests follow the build rules. Every magnetometer mission since has lived by rules of this kind, first written down in documents like this one.
nasa-tm-19670008638-data-book-for-enviro:
NASA's Goddard Space Flight Center in Maryland prepared this data book through its Test and Evaluation Division. The book serves engineers who test spacecraft against the harsh conditions of launch and space. Its preface states the purpose plainly: keep those engineers current and give them a reference that stays up to date.

The opening sections present the status of Goddard satellite programs and NASA launch vehicle and sounding rocket programs. Another section summarizes the test levels then in force for Goddard environmental testing. It also gathers a bibliography of reports on past and current test programs. The volume gathers data on the space and launch settings that spacecraft must survive.
nasa-tm-19670017954-least-squares-analys:
L. Elfenbein, of NASA's Goddard Space Flight Center in Maryland, wrote this analysis on February 3, 1967. It applies the least squares method to tracking data from AS-202, an uncrewed Apollo test flight. The data came from the unified S-band system, which combined tracking, voice, and data links in one radio system for Apollo.

Elfenbein analyzed high-speed range rate and sideways angular data gathered by the Merritt Island and Bermuda ground stations during powered flight. The method fitted smooth polynomials to the tracking data over short time intervals, always in the least squares sense. How far the real data scattered around each fit then measured the noise in the system. The data ran at ten samples per second. The report presents station-by-station results. They give a preliminary picture of the unified S-band system's noise characteristics.
nasa-tm-19680002160-interaction-of-the-m:
Y. C. Whang, at the Goddard Space Flight Center in Maryland, wrote this paper in November 1967. It treats the interaction of the magnetized solar wind with the Moon. The Moon carries no global magnetic shield of its own, so the wind meets the lunar surface almost directly, unlike at Earth.

Explorer 35 had entered lunar orbit in July 1967 to study exactly this encounter. Its results indicated that no detached bow shock wave exists near the Moon. Whang therefore treats the flow theoretically as a free molecule flow of magnetized plasma, deriving the ion density and flux around the Moon. A sizable empty cavity forms just downstream, with plasma changing rapidly across its boundary. Behind the Moon stretches a long wake on the dark side, slightly deflected toward the magnetic field lines. The wake runs about one lunar diameter thick, lengthening far downstream.
nasa-tm-19680027016-applications-of-rada:
Richard F. Broderick, Richard G. Fenner, and Robert Chick, of the Manned Spacecraft Center in Houston, presented this paper in April 1966 at a Southwestern IEEE meeting. They survey how radar serves spacecraft and spaceflight, in programs then flying and in plans still on paper. Gemini, Apollo, and Surveyor had each made radar essential, they open by noting.

Mercury craft carried only beacons that answered ground radar, while Gemini paired radar with a computer to achieve rendezvous. Surveyor used Doppler radar as a landing aid on the Moon. Apollo's lunar module was to carry both rendezvous and landing radars. Planned experiments included side-looking radar, scatterometers, and sharper altimeters and velocity sensors.
nasa-tm-19690004743-effect-of-bleed-syst:
Bobby W. Sanders and Robert W. Cubbison of Lewis Research Center tested inlet bleed systems at Mach 2.50 in this December 1968 memorandum. The axisymmetric mixed-compression inlet uses bleed to control boundary layer air. Two bleed geometries with very different total porous area were compared.

Bleed-exit areas were varied to set different back pressures. At equal supercritical bleed flow, the higher porous-area setup gave higher total-pressure recovery at critical operation. It also cut bleed drag substantially, by the share the authors report. The cost was a complete loss of subcritical stability margin. Careful bleed-exit control let engine airflow drop well below critical without an unstart.
nasa-tm-19690016855-experiences-with-ber:
William Fecych of Lewis Research Center recounts problems with beryllium in the Plum Brook Reactor in this May 1969 memorandum. Intense neutron exposure made major core components swell, distort, and fail. Beryllium parts sat in the reactor's highest neutron fluence regions, where damage ran worst.

Fecych describes the reactor's material surveillance programs in detail. He explains the failure mode of the damaged components. Replacement methods for the swollen parts are laid out step by step. Associated health hazards of handling irradiated beryllium receive attention as well. Distortion is charted against neutron fluence for future planning. The account guides operators of other research reactors facing the same swelling problem.
nasa-tm-19690023855-a-comparison-between:
William E. Shenk and Earl R. Kreins of Goddard Space Flight Center compare observed winds with satellite cloud motions in this July 1969 preprint, X-622-69-285. Their cloud motions come from the Nimbus II satellite's high resolution infrared radiometer, over ocean areas. If drifting clouds faithfully ride the wind, satellites could supply wind data where no weather stations exist.

Motions averaged over two overlapping orbits were checked against wind vectors read from pressure charts. Coastlines in both views corrected the satellite's pointing, and cloud centers fixed each cloud's position. Generally, the authors find, cloud direction stayed within twenty degrees of the wind. Cloud speed stayed within fifteen knots of it as well, a promising verdict.
nasa-tm-19700003621-accelerations-on-24-:
Carl A. Wagner wrote this November 1969 Goddard preprint on accelerations felt by twenty-four-hour satellites. Six such satellites, from Syncom and Early Bird to Intelsat craft, supply tracking records from 1963 through 1969. Sitting in step with Earth's rotation, these craft feel steady pushes from the gravity field's longitude lumps. Those pushes, read carefully, map the field itself.

Wagner reduces the records to thirty-five well determined accelerations from the uneven gravity field. From them he derives two best resonant gravity fields, carried to fourth order. He also relocates the four east-west balance points where a geostationary satellite can rest. Recent gravity models, he notes, clearly improve on the best models of 1966.
nasa-tm-19710002749-the-use-of-automatic:
NASA's Electronics Research Center in Cambridge, Massachusetts, issued this study as document PM-64. It applies automatic control theory and a simple math model of the pilot to helicopter control design. The goal is a manual control system that helps a pilot fly a landing approach on instruments, down to a hover at touchdown.

The work began as a brief one-week investigation in July 1968. Its synthesis technique proved quite successful in that short trial. The method was later used to define flight director control laws for Langley's tandem rotor helicopter. Tests ran on a fixed-base simulator with a nonlinear model of that aircraft, switching between hover and cruise control modes.
nasa-tm-19710014299-process-and-apparatu:
J W Wasquin, Marvin Estes, and David Webb of the Marshall Space Flight Center described a new way to make diamonds in NASA TM X-64543. Their laboratory was the Product Engineering and Process Technology Laboratory. The method synthesizes diamond grit rather than gem stones. Diamond grit serves as a hard abrasive for grinding and smoothing other materials.

The abstract calls the method new and unique. The grit it makes has many crystals joined together. Its sizes match those commonly used in grinding and lapping work. Synthetic grit gave industry a supply that did not depend on mined diamonds. The report shares both the process and the apparatus behind it.
nasa-tm-19710016472-multicolor-photometr:
Thomas Kelsall of the Goddard Space Flight Center completed this work as a 1971 doctoral thesis at the University of Maryland. His adviser was astronomy professor Roger A Bell. Kelsall measured the light of supergiant stars and Cepheid variables through seven color filters. Cepheids pulse in brightness and serve as distance markers in astronomy. Careful color readings reveal their heat and makeup.

Kelsall combined the color readings into new indices. Those indices were built to cancel the reddening caused by dust between the stars. Four such cleaned indices came out of the work. Freed from dust effects, the colors speak more directly about the stars themselves. The thesis prints the full photometry results for both star groups.
nasa-tm-19710018186-estimation-of-shock-:
George E Kaattari of the Ames Research Center wrote this May 1971 memorandum, NASA TM X-62,031. It gives quick methods for estimating the shock layer around a delta wing body space shuttle orbiter. At hypersonic speed, a shock wave wraps the craft in a thin hot layer. Designers need its thickness and the pressure it presses onto the skin.

Kaattari's methods compute the shock tilt angle along the body's center plane. They also give the surface pressure value for bodies held at an angle of attack. The methods suit shapes with oval cross sections. They also suit oblong sections with rounded corners. The usable angle range widens as the body grows more slender.
nasa-tm-19710025818-outgassing-tests-on-:
Lenora B Wells and David C Grana of the Langley Research Center ran these outgassing tests in September 1971, as NASA TM X-2360. They placed a microwave oven and freeze dried foods inside a vacuum chamber. The chamber pressure matched a possible spacecraft cabin level. In a closed cabin, gases leaking from gear and food build up fast. The team needed to know what the oven and meals would release.

The oven gave off mainly two butanol forms and hexane. Most foods released too little gas to identify clearly. Only the chicken chunks produced enough vapor for a firm reading. Their products were hexanal and methyl formate. Such checks helped judge everyday gear for crewed cabins.
nasa-tm-19720017059-a-procedure-for-pred:
Robert N Hosier of the Army Air Mobility laboratory and William H Mayes of the Langley Research Center wrote this noise procedure in May 1972, as NASA TM X-2556. Large blowdown wind tunnels are deafening while they run. Their roar fills the test section and spills over nearby communities. Designers needed a way to predict that noise before building. The procedure covers both the inside and outside fields.

Formulas predict the test section noise level and its spectrum. Two sources are treated, the tunnel burner and the turbulent boundary layer. Outside levels matter for workers and neighbors near the tunnel. The method gives overall levels, not just single tones. Tunnel planners could then add silencing where the numbers demanded. The work joined two Langley based research groups.
nasa-tm-19720017532-pre-emphasis-determi:
G R Wallace of the Marshall Space Flight Center and W E Salter of Sperry Rand Corporation issued these schedules on March 10, 1972, as NASA TM X-64648. Wallace worked in the Astrionics Laboratory. Their subject is pre-emphasis for a telemetry station. Pre-emphasis boosts weak high signals before sending, then trims them on receipt. Done right, it evens out noise across all channels. The station used FM subcarriers on an S-band link.

Eleven fixed bandwidth subcarriers shared the transmitter. The team computed schedules for three receiver signal strengths. Those strengths ranged from weak to comfortably strong. The goal was matching performance at the receiver's middle frequencies. Ground stations for spacecraft telemetry used such schedules daily. The report fixed values engineers could apply directly.
nasa-tm-19720020266-apollo-saturn-c00-00:
Kennedy Space Center issued this technical manual for the Apollo Saturn program. It gives operating and maintenance instructions for one ground system. The system protects communication cables from rusting away underground. Launch complex cables lie buried in soil or sunk in water. Florida's wet, salty ground attacks them constantly. Cathodic protection fights that corrosion with electric current. The manual belongs to the Apollo Saturn operations series.

The method impresses enough direct current onto the cables. That current stops or arrests the corrosion process. Crews maintaining the launch complex worked from these instructions. The system guarded cables at the Cape Kennedy launch area. Reliable communications were essential on launch day. Quiet manuals like this one kept the ground infrastructure alive between missions.
nasa-tm-19720024297-oxygen-hydrogen-inje:
John P. Wanhainen of the Lewis Research Center wrote this NASA memorandum in September 1972. Lewis, in Cleveland, Ohio, studied engines and power for flight. Wanhainen tested an injector, the part that feeds fuel into a rocket chamber. His fuel pair was liquid oxygen and liquid hydrogen.

The tests aimed at a strong, high thrust injector built from tubes set one inside another. He also checked how well the design worked with ablative chambers. Those chambers shed heat by slowly wearing away inside. Results like these helped engineers design rocket parts that could stand great heat and force.
nasa-tm-19720024581-flat-conductor-cable:
W. Angele wrote this NASA memorandum in August 1972 at the Marshall Space Flight Center in Alabama. He worked in the Process Engineering Laboratory there. His subject was flat conductor cable, a ribbon like form of wiring, and the connectors that join it.

Angele describes a connector series whose contacts are each sealed on their own. He covers how the design grew, what it had to meet, and how it was tested. He also deals with cost. Sealed contacts matter where moisture or dirt could spoil an electrical link. The report gave space hardware builders a tested option for compact wiring.
nets-to-catch-the-wind:
Elinor Wylie filled Nets to Catch the Wind with short poems, listed on its contents page one by one. Early titles include Beauty, The Eagle and the Mole, and Madman's Song. August, The Crooked Stick, and Wild Peaches follow. No prose frame joins them in the sample.

Later poems turn to a crowded trolley car, bells in the rain, and winter sleep. Village Mystery, Sunset on the Spire, and Escape keep the mix of town and nature scenes. Fire and Sleet and Candlelight and Blood Feud close the list given here. The titles alone show Wylie's range: bright images, sharp moods, and songs that catch at passing things.
old-mother-west-wind:
Thornton Burgess wrote these animal tales for young children. He dedicated the book to his mother and son. His son's love of stories inspired the tales, he says. The contents list sixteen chapters set in the Green Meadows. Old Mother West Wind sends her Merry Breezes out daily.

Stories explain why Grandfather Frog has no tail. Others tell why Jimmy Skunk wears stripes. Peter Rabbit, Reddy Fox, and Sammy Jay cause gentle trouble. Each tale teaches a small lesson about nature. Its meadow world began Burgess's long Bedtime Story series.
ormond: Ormond is a novel by Maria Edgeworth, dated 1817 in this edition, from the Irish writer whose fiction of manners and education shaped the early nineteenth-century novel. The hosted sample, however, shows nothing of the book itself. It contains only a bare contents list: twenty numbered chapters with no titles given. No opening page, preface, or line of Edgeworth's prose appears. This note therefore records only what the edition's front matter establishes — author, title, date, and chapter count — and makes no claims about Ormond's plot, characters, or themes.
osceola-the-seminole-or-the-red-fawn-of-:
Captain Mayne Reid built his 1858 novel Osceola the Seminole on the brief, heroic struggle of the Seminole chief Osceola against the United States. The publisher's preface argues that the historical novel ranks highest among fictions. It improves the mind while enchanting the senses, the preface says. Readers will sympathize with the gallant spirit who fought for his people's freedom. They will rejoice in the result all the same, the preface promises.

Chapter one opens in rapture over Florida itself, the flowery land named by the Spanish adventurer who sighted it on Palm Sunday. Reid catalogs its virgin forests, fragrant groves of aniseed and orange, myrtle and magnolia, golden water lilies, and towering cypress swamps. Into that Eden of a landscape he sets the tragedy of the Seminole war.
otto-of-the-silver-hand:
Howard Pyle wrote and illustrated Otto of the Silver Hand for young readers, setting his tale of a little boy in the medieval Germany he loved to draw. The chapter titles alone promise a robber-baron world. There is the Dragon's house, and a baron who went forth to shear and came home shorn. One-eyed Hans, a ride for life, and the great Emperor follow.

Pyle's foreword calls the middle ages a black gulf of ignorance, superstition, and cruelty between ancient wisdom and modern light. Yet good people survived in quiet monasteries, he insists, and his hero is a boy who saw both the good and the bad of men. By gentleness and love, not strife and hatred, Otto rises above other men. The book is Pyle's gentlest vision of the age of castles.
our-mutual-friend: Our Mutual Friend is Charles Dickens's last completed novel. The hosted sample shows its contents alone. That contents maps a four-book structure, starting with The Cup and the Lip. Birds of a Feather and A Long Lane follow. Chapter titles name the machinery: the R. Wilfer family, Boffin's Bower, and Podsnappery. Birds of prey are tracked and brought down. No page of Dickens's prose appears in the sample.
outward-bound-or-young-america-afloat-a-: Outward Bound, or Young America Afloat, is a boys' novel by William T. Adams. He wrote as Oliver Optic. Boston published it in 1869, and the frontispiece flies the series banner Young America Abroad. The hosted sample shows only the title pages and a dedication's start. No page of the story itself appears. This note records the book's identity and series, and claims nothing about its voyage.
paris-under-the-commune-the-seventy-thre:
John Leighton's Paris under the Commune chronicles the seventy-three days of the second siege. London published the illustrated volume in 1871, the Commune's own year. Sketches taken on the spot fill it. Portraits come from original photographs. A long quotation from Victor Hugo, dated 1848, stands as its warning. Hugo foretells what a red republic would do to France.

Hugo's prophecy is savage. The red flag would replace the tricolour. The Vendôme Column would be coined into pennies. The assignat press and the guillotine would work together. Leighton's preface begins more quietly. Early in June he was making notes and sketches in Paris. He had no idea what he would do with them. The siege of the Commune decided that for him.
pearl-of-pearl-island: The hosted sample here shows only the front matter of Pearl of Pearl Island, the contents and an opening song, with no story chapters visible. The title page names John Oxenham and the London publishers Hodder and Stoughton, 1908. The contents divide the novel into six parts, from "Pearl" and "Lost Pearl" to "Pearl in a Ring" and "Smaller Pearls." The prefatory verses praise a pearl island in a silver sea.
penguin-island: The hosted sample here shows only the front matter of Penguin Island, the title page and an extensive contents, with no chapter text visible. The contents lay out Anatole France's mock history in eight books, from the life of Saint Maël and the baptism of the penguins, through ancient times, the Middle Ages. Modern times follow. Chapters promise the first clothes, the origin of property, the dragon of Alca, and the metamorphosis of the penguins into a nation.
personal-memoirs-of-a-residence-of-thirt:
Henry R. Schoolcraft's Personal Memoirs, published in 1851, covers thirty years of residence with the Indian tribes on the American frontiers, from 1812 to 1842. His dedicatory letter recalls travelling into the Genesee country when it was called the Garden of the West. That journey led him to deeper and more adventurous inroads into the American wilderness.

Schoolcraft served as an Indian agent and explorer, and his memoirs mix journey notes with brief notices of passing events, facts, and opinions. The book is a first-hand record of the early republic's dealings with Native peoples, written by a man who lived among them.
poison-island:
Arthur Thomas Quiller-Couch, writing as Q, spins a treasure adventure in Poison Island, told by a boy drawn into the orbit of the mysterious Captain Coffin. Chapter titles chart the course: a first meeting with the captain, school at Copenhagen Academy, a street fight, a whaleboat, and a first glimpse of a chart. Murder enters with a crime in a summer-house and a bloodstain on a stile, and the chart of Mortallone becomes the prize everyone hunts.

Captain Coffin's log takes over the telling late in the book, after confessions, cashboxes, and corner cupboards have thickened the plot. Quiller-Couch, the great anthologist, was also a master of the Cornish adventure tale in Stevenson's line. This novel gives boys of its day the full cargo: a map, a mystery, sea captains with secrets, and an island whose name promises danger.
ptolemy-tetrabiblos-ashmand:
Ptolemy's Tetrabiblos, written around 150 CE, is astrology's foundational ancient textbook. J. M. Ashmand's 1822 translation is the classic English version preserved here. Ptolemy was also the greatest astronomer of the ancient world.

Four books lay out planets, signs, aspects, and their supposed influences. Weather, nations, births, and individual fortunes all fall under the system. Ptolemy presents astrology as a physical science of heavenly effects. His authority kept the system dominant for well over a thousand years. Ashmand's translation served generations of English readers and astrologers. The Tetrabiblos also witnesses Hellenistic star science from its most systematic mind. Few books of its kind have been read so long by so many.
rainbow-s-end: Rainbow's End, by Rex Beach, author of The Spoilers and The Iron Trail, is shown here by its title page and contents. The chapters promise a tale of Spanish gold in a valley of delight. The O'Reilly and Retribution open the list. The Spanish Doubloon and Marauders follow. Filibusters comes later. So do The City among the Leaves and The City of Beggars. The hand of the Captain-General is one turn of the plot. A woman with a mission is another.
ramsey-milholland:
Ramsey Milholland, by Booth Tarkington, is dedicated to the memory of Billy Miller, 1908 to 1918, named a little patriot and friend of mankind. Chapter one sets an old man and his small grandson in the shade of a big walnut tree, watching a Decoration Day parade go up the long street.

As the band's tune drifts back, the grandfather murmurs "When Johnnie Comes Marching Home," and the boy questions him about the Civil War. They did not all feel gay, the old man admits, when the army came home. They felt relieved instead. No, they were never afraid the Rebels would win. The talk starts the boy's own story.
religio-medici-hydriotaphia-and-the-lett:
Sir Thomas Browne's Religio Medici, Hydriotaphia, and A Letter to a Friend are printed together here, with an introduction and notes by J. W. Willis Bund. Sampson Low of London issued the edition in 1869. Bund, of Gonville and Caius College, Cambridge, also edited Rochefoucauld's maxims in a companion volume of the same years.

Religio Medici sets out a doctor's faith in Browne's rich, winding prose. Hydriotaphia treats urn burial and what men leave behind them. The Letter to a Friend, written on a death, completes the three. Notes to each work follow the texts, in a book that holds Browne's most loved shorter writings in one place.
romance-island:
Zona Gale published this novel with Bobbs-Merrill of Indianapolis in 1906, with pictures by Hermann C. Wall. A line from Novalis heads it, asking who can fail to believe in magic after a first kind glance from the woman he loves. Dinner Time opens the contents, and A Scrap of Paper follows.

St. George and the Lady and The Prince of Far-Away set the tale's fairy tone. Olivia proposes in the fifth chapter, and Two Little Men, Dusk, and The Porch of the Morning follow. The Lady of Kingdoms, The Isle of Hearts, and a vigil lead toward the Hall of Kings. Open Secrets closes a list steeped in glamour and make-believe.
rosa-s-quest-or-the-way-to-the-beautiful:
Anna Potter Wright wrote this tale for the young, her first book, published by the Moody Press of Chicago under a copyright of 1904. She dedicates it to her mother, who abides in the beautiful land of the title. The contents open with a child's question: How Much is the Fare?

Esther's Perplexity and Rosa's Mother Moves follow, then Life with Mrs. Gray. The last chapters listed are named The Way Sought and The Way Found, showing the quest's shape in their titles. Rosa's search for the road to the beautiful land, and the fare it costs her, carries the story in the manner of a pilgrim tale for children.
sabbath-in-puritan-new-england:
Alice Morse Earle wrote The Sabbath in Puritan New England, shown here in a seventh edition given to the memory of her mother. The contents list twenty-three chapters on the meeting-house and the day. Early heads cover the New England meeting-house, the church militant, summons by drum and horn and shell, old-fashioned pews, and seating the meeting. Later heads treat the tithingman and the sleepers, the length of the service, the icy cold of the meeting-house, the noon-house, the deacon's office, and the psalm-books of the Pilgrims.

Chapter I opens at Plymouth, where the Pilgrim Fathers, on landing, at once assigned a Lord's Day meeting-place for the Separatist church. That first place was a timber fort, both strong and fitted for worship and defense together. From that start Earle's table of heads traces how the Sabbath was kept in strict Puritan towns.
saint-george-for-england:
G. A. Henty addresses Saint George for England to his dear lads in a signed preface. Against the claim that tales of fighting and bloodshed do no good and teach no moral, Henty argues that war has its lessons as well as peace. Such tales, he says, show that resolve and zeal can work marvels, and that true courage goes with magnanimity and gentleness. Courage is the parent of almost all other virtues, since few can be practiced without it. The courage of English forefathers, he holds, built the greatest empire in the world round a small island.

At no period, Henty claims, did England stand so high in Europe as in the time recorded in the volume. A chivalrous king and a still more chivalrous prince filled the whole people with their martial spirit, and English armies won at Cressy and Poitiers and at sea off Sussex.
scenes-in-switzerland:
Scenes in Switzerland was issued by the American Tract Society at 150 Nassau Street, New York, and entered for copyright in 1868. The contents list eight pieces: Gretchen, A Night in the Cathedral, and The Glaciers of Savoy. It also lists The Bride of the Aar, A Sabbath in Lausanne, and The Guide of Montanvert. Mont Blanc and From Berne to Basle close the list. Page numbers run from the opening tale at page five to the closing journey at page one hundred thirty-five. No author is named on the title page shown here.

The first piece, Gretchen, opens with travel. Time flies swiftly when sightseeing, the narrator says, and it was late in the autumn of a year given only as 18-- when the narrator reached Lindau. Lake Constance lay before the traveler as a pale, green sheet of water.
seaward-sussex-the-south-downs-from-end-:
Edric Holmes walked and wrote the South Downs from one end to the other for this Sussex guide, printed in London in 1920. Mary M. Vigers supplied one hundred pictures, while Holmes drew the maps and plans himself. Holmes thanks the county's first sound historian, M. A. Lower, for groundwork.

Town by town and hill by hill, the route takes in old houses, churches, and wide chalk views toward the sea. A Hurstmonceux plate fronts the volume. Walkers and armchair travelers get a full record of a loved landscape as it stood just after the First World War.
seeing-europe-with-famous-authors-volume:
Francis W. Halsey chose and edited this first volume of a ten-volume travel set, covering Great Britain and Ireland. Halsey had edited works on great epochs in American history and on famous orations. Part One opens as a tourist lands at Liverpool, Fishguard, or Plymouth and rides a steamer train toward London.

Famed writers guide the reader place by place, mixing history with close watching of daily life. Drake's defeat of the Spanish Armada and Nelson's call to duty at Trafalgar color the first pages. New travelers got both trip advice and a taste of the lands' past before they ever left home.

Francis W. Halsey edited this second volume of his ten-volume travel set, carrying Great Britain and Ireland into Part Two. The volume turns to English literary shrines, the homes and haunts of famed writers. Named guides include Charles T. Congdon, Theodore F. Wolfe, and William Howitt.

Stops in the contents list include Stoke Poges, Haworth, Gad's Hill, Rydal Mount, and Twickenham. Each place ties a landscape or house to a poet or novelist readers knew well. Later sections move to other English scenes. Book lovers planning a trip could walk ground made rich by the writers they admired.

Francis W. Halsey edited this seventh volume of his travel set, issued by Funk and Wagnalls in 1914. Volume Seven opens Italy, Sicily, and Greece in Part One. A view of the Coliseum and the Arch of Titus fronts the book.

Famed writers lead readers among ruins, churches, and coast towns of the Italian lands. Halsey adds opening notes that frame each place and writer.
