The set's plan gives tourists both sound guidance and fine writing about the ground they cross. Classical history stands close at hand here, since Rome's stones still shape the roads a visitor walks.

Francis W. Halsey edited this eighth volume of his travel set, issued by Funk and Wagnalls with a 1914 copyright. Volume Eight carries Italy, Sicily, and Greece into Part Two. A view of the Parthenon fronts the book, fitting the Greek ground ahead.

Contents continue the tour through Italian and Greek scenes in the words of famed writers. Churches, ruins, islands, and old cities pass in turn, each with its history told by a known guide. Readers who had walked Part One could finish the southern route here, with the same blend of trip help and strong writing.
sermons-on-various-important-subjects-wr:
Rev. Andrew Lee, pastor of the North Church in Lisbon, Connecticut, published these sermons at Worcester in October 1803. Isaiah Thomas Jr. printed and sold the book, as did Lee himself. Many sermons take up hard passages of Scripture and work them through with care.

The first two sermons treat the wisdom of God in the means used to spread the gospel, from a text in First Corinthians. A third argues that the falling away of Christians proves the faith's truth. Early American readers got learned, earnest preaching from a country pulpit, set in print for homes far from Lisbon.
sganarelle-or-the-self-deceived-husband:
Moliere brought out this one-act verse comedy at the Theatre du Petit-Bourbon on May 28, 1660, six months after a great hit with the Precieuses Ridicules. An opening notice in English weighs claims that an Italian farce gave him the first idea. No translator is named in these pages.

Each trifle in the plot turns into seeming proof, taken as solid by both husband and wife. Sganarelle burns to kill the man he thinks wronged him, while cowardice holds his hand. The notice praises the sprightly talk throughout. Jealousy built on air drives one of Moliere's neatest small farces.
sight-to-the-blind:
Lucy Furman wrote this mountain tale, issued in 1914 with an opening essay by Ida Tarbell. Nurses and teachers at a settlement school on Perilous Creek carry health teaching into the hills. Miss Shippen, a trained nurse, rides over Tudor Mountain to the headwaters of Clinch one September morning.

Talks on spitting, typhoid, and nursing reach mothers in a forlorn schoolhouse. A dinner visit leads toward Aunt Dalmanuthy, low in spirits, whose needs give the tale its title and heart. Furman writes Kentucky mountain life with respect, showing settlement workers and hill families learning from each other.
sima-qian-memoires-historiques-chavannes:
Édouard Chavannes printed the second tome of his French Shiji in 1896, holding chapters five through twelve. Sima Qian wrote the work around 91 BCE. These chapters tell how the feudal world of Zhou gave way to one empire, then to the Han house.

Qin unites China, the First Emperor rules and falls, and Xiang Yu fights Liu Bang for the throne. The annals end with Gaozu, the peasant who founded Han. Chavannes notes each hard name and rite with care. The tome covers the most dramatic turn in early Chinese history, in the words of its greatest historian.
sir-dominick-ferrand:
A young writer named Peter Baron races across London in this tale, transcribed from an 1893 Macmillan printing. Editor Mr. Locket has taken Baron's piece for a great magazine, yet only if he will alter it. The curt note stings even as it thrills: no young author had yet won such a door.

Baron fights to seem calm while need drives him on. In a third-class carriage, amid acrid smoke and the underground's roar, the shame of that condition sinks in. The tale probes a proud, poor writer's bargain with the market, where genius must bend or starve.
sir-humphrey-gilbert-s-voyage-to-newfoun:
Edward Hayes told this tale of Sir Humphrey Gilbert's last voyage to Newfoundland, prepared here from a 1910 Collier printing. Hayes commanded the Golden Hind, the only ship of the fleet to reach England. An opening essay sketches Gilbert, who planted England's first colony in North America.

Gilbert, born about 1539, won his charter from Queen Elizabeth in 1578 after a first failed bid cost him his fortune. In August 1583 he claimed St. John's harbor and planted his colony. On the voyage home his ship went down in a storm south of the Azores, and Hayes's record preserves the venture.
sky-island-being-the-further-exciting-ad: L. Frank Baum wrote Sky Island for his sister Mary Louise Brewster, as a sequel to the visit of Trot and Cap'n Bill to the Sea Fairies. The contents trace a trip by magic umbrella to an island in the sky. Chapters name the Boolooroo of the Blues, six snub-nosed princesses, the Blue City, and the Pink Country with Tourmaline, its queen in want. War between Pinks and Blues, the capture of Cap'n Bill, and the fate of the umbrella close the list.
snarleyyow-or-the-dog-fiend: Captain Marryat wrote Snarleyyow; or, The Dog Fiend, and the issue is dated MDCCCXCV, that is, 1895. The opening pages give the title and a bare contents list. Thirty-seven chapters are named by number alone, from Chapter I through Chapter XXXVII, with no heads or summaries to show what each part holds.
snow-blind:
Katharine Newlin Burt, author of The Branding Iron, wrote the novel Snow-Blind. Chapter One opens at noon on a flat land buried deep in snow, rimmed by dark old forest. The snow shines like sun-struck glass, and one low mountain head breaks the flat line to the north. Hugh Garth drops into the cleared space before his hidden cabin door, bright and quick as a clown through paper.

Garth sheds a load of fresh pelts, kicks off his skis, and takes off fur cap and dark glasses. He ducks through the low door in a mood of thwarted anger and slams it behind him. Inside, a stove glows red in the dim room of bark and rough boards. The hand-made chairs, one great carved throne among them, show the charm of work by an unskilled hand.
sologub-the-created-legend:
Trirodov, a schoolteacher with bold plans for a better world, stands at the center of Sologub's novel trilogy in English translation. Around him swirl town gossip, envy, and petty spite. Sologub, a master of Russian Symbolism, blends a fairy tale mood with sharp satire.

Part of the story follows Trirodov's dream of a free colony for children. Part follows the mean talk and plots of the town that wants to crush him. Dream and malice clash on nearly every page. Few Russian novels mix hope, mockery, and strangeness so fully, and the trilogy shows Sologub at his most ambitious.
some-historical-account-of-guinea-its-si: Anthony Benezet wrote Some Historical Account of Guinea, dated 1771. The full title states the plan of the work. It covers the land's lie and its produce. It covers the bent of its people as well. Then comes a probe of the slave trade. Benezet traces its rise and growth. He weighs its nature and its sad effects. He adds fresh printings of noted authors on the theme. A long extract from Granville Sharpe closes the stated plan.
south-wind:
Norman Douglas opens South Wind with a bishop at sea. Thomas Heard is Bishop of Bampopo in Africa. He is feeling sea-sick, and badly so. The sickness vexes him. He holds sickness wrong in every shape. Africa has hurt his stomach and made him near an invalid. That fact shames him. Ill health breeds poor work, he holds.

Well or ill, Heard got through his tasks in a businesslike way. He prized folk who are perfect of their kind. Africa, though, has a touch of spite for white men. She makes hay of their livers when they follow their own lights. Heard has been so perfect a pastor that return looks slim. He half plans to quit the Church for school work. For now he is glad of a plain name.
st-george-for-england:
G. A. Henty speaks straight to his boy readers in Saint George for England. Some may say no good comes from tales of fighting. Believe it not, Henty answers. War has its lessons as well as peace. Such tales teach that resolve can work marvels. True courage comes with a kind and gentle spirit. It parents near all other virtues, he holds.

England stood at no time higher in Europe's eyes. That claim frames the tale's age. A king full of knightly spirit led the folk. A prince yet more knightly stood beside him. Their fire lit the whole people. English armies for a time could not be beat. Cressy and Poitiers owe part to better leading and drill. The sea win off Sussex needs the courage account more. Henty drew his facts from Froissart and other writers of the time.
st-ives-being-the-adventures-of-a-french:
Robert Louis Stevenson told St. Ives, the adventures of a French prisoner in England, aloud to his stepdaughter Mrs. Strong, who took it down between January 1893 and October 1894. A note signed S. C. tells that tale's odd birth. Some six weeks before his death, Stevenson laid St. Ives aside to take up Weir of Hermiston. The thirty chapters he had written, the last few not revised, brought the tale within sight of its end.

The course of the rest was known in outline to Mrs. Strong. For readers who dislike a tale left undone, the fine task of writing the missing chapters was given to Mr. Quiller-Couch, whose work starts at Chapter XXXI. The second edition came from William Heinemann at London in 1898, after a first edition of May 5, 1897, reprinted the next day. Chapter I bears the head A Tale of a Lion Rampant.
stage-land: Jerome K. Jerome gives Stage-Land to the earnest student of the drama, that highly respectable but needlessly retiring person of whom we hear much and see so little. Jerome calls his small book comparatively truthful. The contents sort the stock folk of the stage into heads: the hero, the villain, the heroine, and the comic man. The lawyer, the adventuress, the servant girl, the child, the comic lovers, the peasants, the good old man, the Irishman, the detective, and the sailor follow.
station-amusements-in-new-zealand:
Lady Barker wrote Station Amusements in New Zealand as a mate to Station Life. That first book came out three years before. Folk took its plain account of New Zealand life with warmth. Their warmth spurred her to widen the theme. The first book dwelt on things of use. These pages give their whole space to idle hours. A settler's free time forms their theme.

Many readers have friends and kin in those far islands. Such folk will care to know their loved ones' lives. Few books gave their makers so much joy, Barker adds. Few seemed so near to write themselves as these. Chapter I bears the head A Bush Picnic. It opens on a question put since her return to England. Friends ask how she amused herself at the station. Her first answer is that all were too busy. No one there needed amusement, she tells them.
station-life-in-new-zealand:
Lady Barker gives her letters in Station Life in New Zealand, dated 1883, with a frank preface signed F. N. B. The letters, she owns, justly draw the charge of self-regard and smallness of theme. Yet she saw no way to shed those faults without cutting their worth as the exact account of a lady's lot in the brighter, less work-bound side of settling a new land.

No guide or handbook for the would-be migrant is meant, she warns; that reader has a shelf of his own, and will find here scarce one count of goods or folk. The letters record the trips, bold deeds, and sudden calls that broke up the daily life of a New Zealand sheep-farmer's wife, each written while the newness of the scene was fresh. Letter I tells of two months at sea and Melbourne, dated September 22, 1865, from the Port Phillip Hotel.
stories-by-english-authors-england:
Stories by English Authors: England collects The Box Tunnel by Charles Reade, Minions of the Moon by F. W. Robinson, The Four-Fifteen Express by Amelia B. Edwards, The Wrong Black Bag by Angelo Lewis, The Three Strangers by Thomas Hardy, Mr. Lismore and the Widow by Wilkie Collins, and The Philosopher in the Apple Orchard by Anthony Hope.

Reade starts with a train gliding from Paddington on May 7, 1847, and a close look at two passengers in a first-class carriage. Trains, widows, strangers at a cottage door, and small-town puzzles give the volume its spread of English scenes, mixing suspense with quiet character study from well-known pens.
stories-by-english-authors-ireland:
Stories by English Authors: Ireland gathers The Gridiron by Samuel Lover, The Emergency Men by George H. Jessop, A Lost Recruit by Jane Barlow, The Rival Dreamers by John Banim, Neal Malone by William Carleton, and The Banshee by an unnamed writer.

Lover's first tale turns on an old gentleman in the west of Ireland who loved claret, fox-hunting, and drawing out his servant Pat's tales of travel. Pat, a trusted and talkative man, could even talk his master out of a rash dismissal. Comic speech, folk belief, and Irish country life run through the set, from kitchen humor to the wail of the banshee.
studies-from-court-and-cloister-being-es: Only the front pages of an old electronic text are present here. They carry the standard welcome, copyright cautions, and donation appeals of that early free-text project, ending with a title line for Studies from Court and Cloister and the author name J. M. Stone, with a release date of August 2003. No title page, contents, or essay text from Stone's book itself appears in these pages.
supply-and-demand:
Hubert D. Henderson wrote Supply and Demand, dated 1922, with an introduction by J. M. Keynes. Henderson sets out the basic workings of prices and markets in plain terms for the general reader, in a short book of close argument.

The first chapter sketches the economic world: theory and fact, the division of labor, the existence of order, joint products, and capital. The second states the general laws of supply and demand. It warns against loose talk of increases in demand. It follows how changes in each react on price. Odd cases and the trade cycle come in too. A third chapter takes up utility and the margin of consumption, where buyers decide what one more unit is worth to them.
synthetic-tannins-their-synthesis-indust:
Georg Crasser, a doctor of philosophy and lecturer in tanning chemistry at the German Technical College at Brunn, wrote Synthetic Tannins: Their Synthesis, Industrial Production and Application. His preface explains that while Emil Fischer had outlined how natural tannins could be built up, the chemical industry made them in bulk.

Crasser credits the Badische Anilin und Soda-fabrik at Ludwigshafen-on-the-Rhine with finding the means of production, and notes that no list of the synthetic tannins then known had yet been published. His own years at that firm gave him deep practice. His wartime post added more. He served as technical consultant to the Austrian Hide and Leather Commission. The book records what that practice taught him. It surveys the new factory-made tanning agents that were replacing bark and other plant extracts in the leather trade.
t-mann-der-zauberberg-erster-band:
A three-week visit turns into seven years for Hans Castorp at a Davos sanatorium in Der Zauberberg, given here in German, First Volume. The Magic Mountain opens with a young Hamburg engineer arriving above the world of the flatlands. Fever, rest cures, and extraordinary talkers slowly dissolve his sense of ordinary time.

Settembrini the humanist and Naphta the radical debate civilization across Castorp's bed and table. Love for a Russian fellow patient, Clawdia, completes his strange education. Mann builds the twentieth century's most important German novel out of idleness and ideas. The first volume ends with carnival night and a borrowed pencil, small keys to a vast book. Everything here leans toward the storm gathering below.
t-mann-der-zauberberg-zweiter-band:
Hans Castorp's education continues in the Second Volume of Der Zauberberg, in Mann's German. Snowstorms, seances, arrivals, and a fatal duel crowd the mountain's timeless calm as the years pile up unnoticed. The sanatorium's little world darkens toward the catastrophe waiting in the flatlands below.

Debates between Settembrini and Naphta sharpen into violence; love and death trade places in Castorp's famous snow vision. Then the guns of 1914 call him down at last into a war the reader knows better than he does. Mann's philosophical epic closes as Europe's old world ends. The two volumes together form a summit of world literature. In the original German, its sentences roll like the weather over Davos.
the-analysis-of-mind: Only series front matter is present for The Analysis of Mind by Bertrand Russell, dated 1921 and issued in the Muirhead Library of Philosophy. The pages print that library's program, first worded by its late editor, Professor J. H. Muirhead, in 1890. The plan traces modern thought by schools such as sensationalist, realist, and idealist, and by subjects running from the study of mind and morals to art, politics, and theology. None of Russell's own chapters appear in these pages.
the-apology-of-the-church-of-england:
John Jewel, Bishop of Salisbury, wrote this defence of the Church of England, shown in an 1888 edition from Cassell and Company. An introduction explains the book's great interest: Jewel wrote in Latin so that all Europe could read England's answer at the start of Queen Elizabeth's reign. Critics had charged that the Reformation set up a brand-new church.

Jewel's reply, the introduction says, was that the English reformers went back to the old church rather than founding a new one. He set out to prove it from the first centuries of Christian faith. The very word apology then meant a pleading that beats back a charge, and Jewel's Latin title is given as Apologia Ecclesiae Anglicanae.
the-back-of-the-north-wind:
George MacDonald wrote this tale of a small boy and the North Wind in 1871. Its full name is At the Back of the North Wind. MacDonald was a Scots priest whose tales for the young veil deep thought on God and death.

Diamond, a poor cab man's son, is borne at night on the back of the grand North Wind. She is vast, fair, and kind, yet her work brings storms, wrecks, and death in its time. The book is the most loved of MacDonald's tales for the young, and a sad, sweet one.
the-banner-boy-scouts-afloat-or-the-secr:
George A. Warren published a scout adventure in 1913 built around a trip to Cedar Island. Chapter headings start with mysterious boxes and glorious news, then a departure faced with talk of a ghost. The boys lay in stores and start their cruise after ten o'clock.

Trouble on the water follows: a boat stuck in mud, a water gauge, a swift river, and snags to dodge. On the island they find footprints in the sand and try to work out what they mean. Later headings promise orders to leave, movement under darkness, and a camp mystery tied to the secret named in the title.
the-battle-ground:
Ellen Glasgow dedicated her novel to the beloved memory of her mother and divided it into books named Golden Years and Young Blood. Early chapters include a coming of a boy, a house with an open door, a school for gentlemen, and college days.

In the second book a major's Christmas, Betty dreaming by a fire, and Dan and Betty set a romance in motion. Love in a maze, a major losing his temper, and a meeting on a turnpike follow. Betty's unbelief, the Montjoy blood, a road at midnight, and a night of fear lead toward a hush before a storm in the final listed heading.
the-book-of-three-hundred-anecdotes-hist: The Book of Three Hundred Anecdotes is a new set of short tales, classed as drawn from past events, from books, and from humor. Burns and Oates put it out in London, at Granville Mansions, and in New York, on Barclay Street. Only the start of the A-to-Z index is shown. Its heads run from Abernethy and Abon Hannifah to Actors, Affection, and Artists. Tales touch Dr. Adam and a schoolboy, and Atterbury in the House of Peers.
the-boss-and-the-machine-a-chronicle-of-:
Samuel P. Orth wrote The Boss and the Machine, a chronicle of politicians and party organization. Its chapters trace the rise of the party, then the rise of the machine,. The Politician and the City, Tammany Hall, and Lesser Oligarchies come next. Party reform and the expert at last close the book.

Orth starts with a blunt claim: the party system is a core tool of rule by the people. Where power rests on the will of the folk, he says, the party speaks for that will. Parties also came before free rule in most lands. Long before the American colonies formed the United States, England split into Tory and Whig. In the colonies those names marked two views: Tory faith in the King, Whig faith in Parliament. Harsh Tory acts, he says, drove Whigs to revolt.
the-children-of-france-a-book-of-stories: Ruth Royce wrote these stories of young French patriots in the Great War, published in Philadelphia by the Henry Altemus Company in 1918. Only the title page and contents are present here. The chapters tell of Remi the brave, a heroine of Fort Montere, Francois outwitting the Prussians, the sacrifice of little Pierre, a child despatch bearer, and Marie the courageous.The work's own pages are not present here.
the-coming-conquest-of-england: August Niemann wrote this invasion novel, translated by J. H. Freese. Only the title page and contents are present here. The chapters move from a council of state and an officers' mess to a Circassian beauty. The Maharajah, the Pamirs, and the German Emperor follow. Mobilisation, the camp of Lahore, and a battle close what is listed.The chapters themselves remain out of view.
the-common-people-of-ancient-rome-studie:
Frank Frost Abbott, Kennedy Professor of Latin at Princeton University, wrote these studies of Roman life and literature for general readers. Charles Scribner's Sons published the book at New York, copyrighted in 1911. A prefatory note ties it to his earlier volume on society and politics in ancient Rome.

Both books, Abbott says, deal with the life of the common people: their language and literature, their occupations and amusements, and their social, political, and economic conditions. We care about Rome's common people, he argues, because they made the empire what it was. They bore Roman arms from the Euphrates to the Atlantic. Abroad they lived as traders, farmers, and soldiers, holding and Romanizing the provinces. At home they worked as carpenters, masons, and bakers, supplying the capital's daily needs. A transcriber's note explains a stand-in character for the denarius symbol used through the text.
the-complete-works-of-artemus-ward-part-: Part 4 of the Artemus Ward series points toward California, though the record title breaks off mid-phrase. Charles Farrar Browne wrote the Ward pieces. Here, a Gutenberg header takes the place of his pages, offering copyright notes and a plea for donations instead. With no tale text present, the California material cannot be summed up.
the-coral-island:
R. M. Ballantyne's The Coral Island, dated 1858, is told by Ralph Rover, whose ruling passion has been roving since childhood. Ralph was born on the broad Atlantic in a night of storm. His father, grandfather, and great-grandfather all went to sea, and his mother sailed with his father on long voyages.

The family settled in a fishing village on the west coast of England, but Ralph's urge to wander only grew. He shipped in the coasting trade, where sailors' tales of foreign lands fired him most when they turned to the coral islands of the Southern Seas. Those isles were built by a small creature. They were rich in fruit under near-endless summer. Yet they were home, he heard, to wild and bloodthirsty men. At fifteen he resolved to sail there, and won his parents' consent.
the-coxon-fund:
Henry James wrote The Coxon Fund, here in the Martin Secker edition first published in London in 1915, with a text following the Definitive Edition. An unnamed narrator tells the tale. Riding back to the station one evening, he tells himself that his friends have got Mr. Saltram for life.

Alone in the train from Wimbledon to Waterloo, he softens the claim. The Mulvilles will not keep a monopoly of Saltram. Many people will sooner or later have the honor of dealing with him whole. Saltram is to stay all winter with the Mulvilles, whose patience the narrator admires. At dinner that first evening the guest wore new, mostly purple slippers of some queer carpet-stuff, while his hosts still feared higher bidders might snatch him away.
the-crimes-of-england: Gilbert K. Chesterton published The Crimes of England in 1916. Its contents lay out the argument chapter by chapter: first, words to a German professor on the mistakes of German controversialists and where England is really wrong. Then comes the Protestant hero, on Frederick the Great and German influence in England. Then the enigma of Waterloo weighs how England helped Napoleon. It contrasts the religious resistance of Austria and Russia with the irreligion of Prussia and England. Only the title page and the start of this detailed contents are present here.
the-crimson-blind: Fred. M. White's The Crimson Blind, dated 1905, is shown here only through its contents, which list thirty-five chapters. The titles hint at a mystery: Who Speaks?, The Voice in the Darkness, No. 218, Brunswick Square, Hatherly Bell, The House of the Silent Sorrow, Margaret Sees a Ghost, and The Man with the Thumb Again. Two chapters share the book's own title. Only the title page and contents are present here, so the story itself does not appear.
the-customs-of-old-england: The pages present for The Customs of Old England consist of a publisher's list headed Uniform with this Volume. It names other books issued alike in format, among them Marie Corelli's The Mighty Atom, W. W. Jacobs's Light Freights, Arnold Bennett's The Card and The Regent, Jack London's White Fang, Joseph Conrad's Under Western Eyes, and Edgar Rice Burroughs's Tarzan of the Apes. No title page, author name, or text of the work itself appears here.
the-dock-rats-of-new-york-or-the-smuggle:
Early pulp thrills fill The Dock Rats of New York; or, The Smuggler Band's Last Stand, by Old Sleuth, the pen name of Harlan Page Halsey. A 1908 printing as Adventure Series number 76 is noted at the front. Chapter one opens on a calm night shore, where Spencer Vance grabs a boat's rope and hears a sharp cry to hold.

A barefoot girl in rags, bound with a leather belt, steps into the moonlight. She warns him off the boat and draws him into a smuggler plot. Fast talk, disguise, and chase carry this dime-novel style tale.
the-eskdale-herd-boy-a-scottish-tale-for:
Mrs. Blackford's The Eskdale Herd-Boy, a Scottish tale for the instruction and amusement of young persons, tells of John Telfer. Its contents sum up the first chapters: John loses his parents, Pastor Martin befriends him, and Mr. Laurie hires him as herd-boy. Helen Martin's first try at riding gives her mother a text on grit and self-command.

Later heads promise Border lore, a minister's rounds, and a dog's sagacity. Eskdale's hills and farms frame the boy's growth. The tale teaches by scene and talk, in the Sunday-school mode of its age: kind, plain, and fond of nature.
the-feast-of-st-friend:
Arnold Bennett wrote The Feast of St. Friend as a Christmas book, printed at New York in 1911. Its chapters move from the fact of a changed Christmas to praise of feasting and the gift of oneself.

Bennett opens with a claim: something has happened to Christmas, or to our hearts. In old days, he says, the feast stirred homes for weeks, with secrets, parcels, and waits singing in the cold. On the great day, even toothache fled. He longs to bring back that warmth, and ends with the year's last day and the hope of a feast kept for friends.
the-flower-of-the-mind:
Alice Meynell chose and made The Flower of the Mind as a choice among the best poems of English verse. It was printed at London in 1898. The run was two hundred and fifty copies. Her introduction defends the bold plan.

Meynell grants that small sets of poems on one theme appear all the time. But a general choice is a rare thing. Hers runs from Chaucer to Wordsworth and is judged by quality alone. She owns the pride such a task needs. She calls poetry her second life. The book sorts the great English line by one poet-critic's taste. It honors some names and passes others by.
the-flying-u-s-last-stand:
B. M. Bower wrote The Flying-U's Last Stand as a later tale of the Happy Family crew, with Andy Green and the Kid in lead parts. The contents run to past twenty chapters of fights and schemes.

New ways press on old range life: the crew turn nesters, a colony of settlers comes in, and shacks and stock are moved by force. Florence Grace Hallman speaks plainly in one head, and a lost child turns the crew's hearts in another. Bower shows the open-range cow outfit in its last fight against fences, farms, and land sharks.
the-glories-of-ireland: Joseph Dunn and P. J. Lennox edited The Glories of Ireland. Both were professors at the Catholic University of America. The book is dated 1914. It is dedicated to the Irish race in every land. Only front matter is present here. It gives the title page, the editors' note of November 1914, and the start of the contents. The contents name opening essays. They name The Romance of Irish History by Sir Roger Casement. They name The Island of Saints and Scholars. They also name Irish Monks in Europe.
the-gloved-hand: Burton E. Stevenson wrote The Gloved Hand. It is a detective story, dated 1913. Pictures are by Thomas Fogarty. A note says the tale first ran in The Popular Magazine. There it was called The Mind Master. Only front matter is present here. It gives the title page, a list of Stevenson's other books, and the start of a contents list. The first heads run from The Falling Star and A Strange Neighbour. They run to A Call for Help and The Scream in the Night.
the-golden-legend:
Henry Wadsworth Longfellow wrote The Golden Legend. It is a poem in dramatic form. Its prologue is set on the spire of Strasburg Cathedral. It is night, and a storm rages. Lucifer tries to tear down the iron cross. The cross mocks him from its height. He calls on the powers of the air to help.

Voices answer that the saints guard the cross. Guardian angels throng round it. They defeat the spirits everywhere. The cathedral bells ring out their Latin lines. They praise the true God and call the people. They mourn the dead and drive off plague. Lucifer orders his hosts to seize the bells. The voices reply that the bells were baptized with holy water. They defy his utmost power. The prologue opens the poem's fight between heaven and hell.
the-gun-brand: James B. Hendryx wrote The Gun-Brand. A. L. Burt Company published it in New York in 1917, with a frontispiece in colors by Clyde Forsythe. Only front matter is present here. It gives the title page and the start of a contents list. The frontispiece caption reads: The next instant his arms were pinioned to his sides. The heads open with The Call of the Raw and Vermilion Shows His Hand. They name Pierre Lapierre, Brute MacNair, and A Shot in the Night. No chapter text is present.
the-gutenberg-webster-s-unabridged-dicti:
Webster's Revised Unabridged Dictionary, in the version published in 1913 by the C. & G. Merriam Co. of Springfield, Mass., under the direction of Noah Porter, is a large reference work for English words. The portion here covers the letter P. It opens with a short account of the letter itself, its sound, its form, and its links to the letters b, f, and v.

Entries then run in alphabetical order, giving spelling, pronunciation, word origin, and meanings. Early entries include Pa, Paage, Paard, and Pabulum, with notes on law, farming, and daily speech. Older uses are marked, sources are named, and cross references point the reader to related words and to the guide to pronunciation.
the-happy-end:
Joseph Hergesheimer wrote The Happy End, a set of short stories. In a dedication, he says the stories have one purpose, to give pleasure, and that they were made into a book at the request of readers he had pleased. He jokes that he is responsible, in the end, to his grocer, who brought him food in hard times.

The contents list Lonely Valleys, The Egyptian Chariot, The Flower of Spain, Tol'able David, Bread, Rosemary Roselle, and The Thrush in the Hedge. Lonely Valleys opens at a rectory, where a maid in a starched cap admits guests with clear ill will and reports that Doctor Goodlowe has hardly started dinner.
the-hermit-of-far-end:
Margaret Pedler wrote The Hermit of Far End. The book was first published in 1920. A prologue opens in a small room under a roof. The room sits high in Wallater's Buildings. Logs burn quietly in the grate. London traffic reaches the room as a dull murmur.

A woman sits in a low chair by the hearth. Her hands are folded on her knees. She looks toward the door with patient expectation. She touches a slight ring mark on her finger. She murmurs that he will come. He promised to come if she sent the little pearl ring. Sunlight then falls on her worn, lined face.
the-high-school-freshmen-or-dick-co-s-fi:
H. Irving Hancock wrote The High School Freshmen, subtitled Dick & Co.'s First Year Pranks and Sports. Chapter titles include The High School Sneak, Captain of the Hounds, The Muckers and the Gentleman, Dick & Co. Give Football a New Boost, and The Capture of the Bank Robbers. Chapter one opens with a hot denial in a school crowd.

Fred Ripley accuses Dick Prescott to his face, and Dick, cheeks red, answers quietly that he did not do the thing named. Ripley sneers and demands who did the contemptible thing, then. About forty boys from all classes at Gridley High School stand watching the quarrel. A charge of sneaking, locker trouble, and freshman pride set the first-year tale in motion.
the-high-school-pitcher-or-dick-co-on-th:
The High School Pitcher, subtitled Dick & Co. on the Gridley Diamond, is a school baseball story. No author is named in the pages present. Chapter titles include The Principal Hears Something About Pennies, The Call to the Diamond, Trying Out the Pitchers, A Dastard's Work in the Dark, and The Agony of the Last Big Game. Chapter one opens in the big assembly room of Gridley High School.

A bell rings, study noise stops, and a new principal steps to his desk on the platform. He is tall, thin, and severe, about thirty-two or thirty-three. Dr. Carl Thornton, the beloved principal for ten years, is away through ill health. A changed school, a pitching contest, and mean tricks in the dark shape the season's tale.
the-hilltop-boys-on-lost-island: Cyril Burleigh wrote The Hilltop Boys on Lost Island. The book was published in Cleveland in 1917. Burleigh is named as the author of The Hilltop Boys. The contents list adventure chapters. Early titles include The Floating Academy. Later titles include Jack's Daring Rescue and Caught on Lost Island. The list goes on to A Walk Under Water. It ends with In the Lair of the Fox. Nothing past the front matter is present here. The adventure itself does not appear.
the-holiday-round:
A. A. Milne wrote The Holiday Round, published in London in 1912, and he is named as the author of The Days' Play. The contents group light pieces under headings such as Holiday Time, The House-Warming, At Play, Two Stories, An Odd Lot, Little Plays for Amateurs, and Stories of Successful Lives. Holiday Time opens with The Ordeal by Water.

A voice at the back of the narrator's neck announces that they will now bathe. He grunts and tries to hold a jolly dream in which nobody got up early. Archie repeats the order, sits on his knees, and puts a damp towel on his face. Seaside mornings, games, and small social trials fill the pieces in a comic register.
the-hollow-land:
William Morris wrote The Hollow Land, opening with a verse from the Niebelungen Lied in Carlyle's rendering, about heroes in great glory and wonders many told. A section headed Struggling in the World begins with a question from an old narrator: do you know where the Hollow Land is?

The narrator, Florian of the house of the Lilies, has sought the land for long years, since there he first saw his love. Memory brings trumpets over desolate moors, clashing horse-hoofs, and the glitter of steel. His father was lord of his house, then his eldest brother Amald. Morris frames a tale of striving, misunderstanding, and a dreamed land of cool waves and roses.
the-hollow-of-her-hand: George Barr McCutcheon wrote The Hollow of Her Hand. The contents list nineteen chapters, among them March Comes in Like the Lion, The Passing of a Night, Hetty Castleton, While the Mob Waited, Southlook, The Ghost at the Feast, Mr. Wrandall Perjures Himself, and Sara Wrandall Finds the Truth. A frontispiece line shows a speaker dividing two piles of clothes between herself and a sleeping girl. Only the title page and contents are present here, so the novel itself does not appear.
the-house-of-the-misty-star-a-romance-of: Frances Little, the pen name printed here with Fannie Caldwell Macaulay and already attached to The Lady of the Decoration, published this romance with the Century Company in New York in 1915. Its subtitle promises a romance of youth and hope and love in old Japan, and the volume is dedicated to a faithful friend, Nui Shiome of Tokio. Only the title pages and the start of the contents are present here, so the story itself does not appear. One illustration caption survives, showing a woman quickly crossing burning coal.
the-kingdom-of-the-blind:
E. Phillips Oppenheim opens this wartime novel in the Ritz lounge. Lady Anselman stands counting her guests. Her finger is delicately poised as she counts. A great French actress chats nearby. A pale man speaks perfect French with her. A Cabinet Minister wears a schoolboy's air at an illicit feast. Geraldine Conyers talks with a famous musician. A naval lieutenant banters with a petite girl. Twice the hostess counts and frowns. She is one short. She cannot remember whom they await.

The missing guest is Ronnie, who can only just get about. Her patter introduces Surgeon-Major Thomson among the company. He inspects hospitals at the front. Oppenheim builds his spy story inside a dinner party. Twelve covers wait, with one place empty. London society glitters in the room. The war presses at its edges.
the-letters-of-norah-on-her-tour-through: Mrs. McDougal wrote letters from Ireland as special correspondent for the Montreal Witness under the name Norah. Only the title page and a long list of subscribers who funded the book publication are present here, naming donors in Montreal, Toronto, Belleville, and Paris. Sums beside the names range from one dollar to ten dollars. The travel letters themselves, describing Ireland for Canadian readers, cannot be seen in this record beyond that subscription list.
the-life-of-kit-carson-hunter-trapper-gu:
Edward S. Ellis wrote his life of Kit Carson, hunter, trapper, guide, Indian agent, and colonel in the United States Army. His introduction argues that Carson real worth showed best to close companions. Integrity, bravery, loyalty, quick judgment in danger, and woodcraft marked the man, Ellis says.

Carson served as counselor to Fremont on Rocky Mountain expeditions and won Native trust by speaking with a single tongue. Ellis says he averted outbreaks and won justice for Native people where others failed. Chapter one turns to Carson youth after an admiring, openly heroic introduction.
the-magic-pudding-being-the-adventures-o:
Norman Lindsay's The Magic Pudding tells the adventures of Bunyip Bluegum, a koala, with his friends Bill Barnacle and Sam Sawnoff. The book introduces Bunyip from front, side, and back: a fine, round, splendid fellow. Beside him stands his Uncle Wattleberry, more square than round, whose whiskers fill the pictures. Those whiskers, the narrator explains, were the main reason Bunyip left home to see the world.

Their tree-house was too small for the whiskers. The whiskers were red, blew about in the wind, and got into the soup at dinner, so tidy Bunyip had to eat outside while lizards borrowed his soup. Lindsay tells the tale in prose mixed with verse, with the uncle's whiskers treated as a serious domestic grievance.
the-magic-speech-flower-or-little-luke-a: Melvin Hix wrote The Magic Speech Flower, or Little Luke and His Animal Friends, published by Longmans, Green, and Company with an October 1912 first publication. Only the title pages and a publisher's advertisement for Hix's Once-Upon-A-Time Stories are present here, so Luke's story itself does not appear. Hix is identified as principal of Public School 9 in Long Island City and co-author of the Horace Mann Readers. The advertisement says his retold stories aim to interest pupils in the first and second grades.
the-man-in-lonely-land:
Kate Langley Bosher, author of Mary Cary, published The Man in Lonely Land in 1912 and dedicated it to her brother. Chapter one, headed General, opens on Mr. Winthrop Laine coming home in vile weather. He throws his gloves on the table, his hat on the desk, and his overcoat on a chair. Then he looks down at soaking wet shoes. He swears that two weeks of rain, sleet, and snow would ruin any temper. The contents thread a Dorothea through Laine's lonely life: Dorothea and Mr. Laine, a letter from Dorothea, Dorothea asks questions, and a visit from Dorothea.

Other chapters promise the loss of his best friend, Christmas shopping, a visit to Virginia, and springtime. Bosher sets a solitary man's orderly, wet evening at the start of a story plainly headed toward company.
the-mississippi-bubble-how-the-star-of-g:
Emerson Hough's 1902 novel The Mississippi Bubble is present here only in title page, dedication, and contents, with no story text. Its long subtitle promises the rise and fall and rise again of John Law of Lauriston's fortune, worked by a woman's grace. Henry Hutt supplied the illustrations, and the dedication reads simply To L.C.H.

Book I's seventeen chapters, the only part listed, begin with The Returned Traveler and At Sadler's Wells. John Law of Lauriston and The Point of Honor follow, with divers employments and a resolution for Law. Catharine Knollys enters at Chapter VIII, and quarrels, felony, prisoners, and an escape carry the list to its close at Whither.
the-misuse-of-mind:
Karin Stephen's The Misuse of Mind, published in London and New York in 1922, studies Henri Bergson's attack on intellectualism, the habit of trusting abstract reason alone. Stephen had been a Fellow of Newnham College, Cambridge. Three chapters are listed: Explanation, Fact, and Matter and Memory.

A prefatory letter from Bergson himself, printed in French, heads the volume. He calls her reading of his work personal and original, valuable in its own right apart from his texts. Her distinction between fact and matter, he writes, let her draw his scattered views into a unity with strong logical rigour. The letter, dated as a prefatory note, gives the study an unusual blessing from its subject.
the-modern-scottish-minstrel-volume-1-th:
Only illustrated title pages are present here for volume 1 of The Modern Scottish Minstrel, edited by Charles Rogers and published in Edinburgh by Adam and Charles Black. No songs and no poet memoirs appear. The full title promises the songs of Scotland of the past half century, with memoirs of the poets.

The frontispiece shows the Auld House o' Gask, birthplace of Lady Nairn, copied by permission of Patterson and Sons. A second illustration gives a lithographed portrait of Sir Walter Scott, made for the volume by Schenck and McFarlane. Rogers's credentials, doctor of laws and fellow of the Society of Antiquaries of Scotland, are printed beneath his name on the title page.
the-modern-scottish-minstrel-volume-2-th:
Volume 2 of The Modern Scottish Minstrel, edited by Charles Rogers and published in Edinburgh by Adam and Charles Black, is present here only as illustrated title pages. No songs, sketches, or specimens appear. The title repeats the promise of the songs of Scotland of the past half century, with memoirs of the poets.

This volume's pictures differ from its siblings. The frontispiece shows Altrive, the residence of the Ettrick Shepherd, the poet James Hogg. A lithographed portrait of Hogg follows, copied from an original in his widow's possession by Schenck and McFarlane of Edinburgh, with his signature beneath. The title page wording otherwise matches volume 1 of the same set.
the-modern-scottish-minstrel-volume-3-th:
Illustrated title pages alone are present here for volume 3 of The Modern Scottish Minstrel, edited by Charles Rogers and published in Edinburgh by Adam and Charles Black. The songs themselves, and the memoirs of the poets the title promises, do not appear in these pages. Scotland's songs of the past half century remain the stated subject.

Abbotsford, Sir Walter Scott's home, serves as this volume's frontispiece subject. The second illustration is a lithographed portrait of the poet Allan Cunningham, made for the Minstrel by Schenck and McFarlane. The full title adds sketches and specimens of the poets to the memoirs named on the earlier volumes' title pages. Nothing beyond these leaves is shown.
the-modern-scottish-minstrel-volume-4-th:
Volume 4 of The Modern Scottish Minstrel, edited by Charles Rogers and published in Edinburgh by Adam and Charles Black, appears here only in illustrated title pages. No song texts and no lives of poets are present. The full title again promises the songs of Scotland of the past half century, with memoirs, sketches, and specimens of the poets.

The frontispiece is headed simply Campbell, naming the poet Thomas Campbell as its subject. A lithographed portrait of the poet Henry Scott Riddell, made for the volume by Schenck and McFarlane, forms the second illustration. Title wording matches the earlier volumes of Rogers's set, which are likewise represented by their opening leaves alone.
the-motor-girls-on-cedar-lake-or-the-her:
The Motor Girls on Cedar Lake, subtitled The Hermit of Fern Island, opens with Chapter I, Pushing Off, at a lakeside camp. Cora Kimball, the hostess, greets Bess Robinson and her twin sister Belle. Jack, Cora's brother, had predicted Belle would fall for a clump of white birches and paint on bark; Cora bets instead on the pines. No author is named on the pages shown here.

More important news follows: Cora's new motor boat has just arrived, and no boy is on the premises to show her how to run it. Jack is absent, and Cora refuses to wait until evening. Since the twins took the first spin in her automobile, the Whirlwind, they are invited to share the boat's trial run too.
the-mysterious-island:
Jules Verne's The Mysterious Island is presented here in the translation by Stephen W. White, and a long editor's note explains why that matters. The familiar English version by W. H. G. Kingston, the note says, altered the closing chapters beyond recognition. Captain Nemo's appearance was rewritten, and every mention of his earlier life as a fighter for Indian independence was removed.

White's version saw print first in Philadelphia's Evening Telegraph and as an 1876 reprint book, set by hand for a newspaper. The editors corrected obvious printers' errors while keeping period spelling. They call White's the most faithful translation, never reprinted until now. The title pages promise a full glossary and a map of the island, under a heading naming the book Verne's last story.
the-norwegian-account-of-haco-s-expediti:
A Norwegian account of King Haco's expedition against Scotland in the year 1263 survives in Icelandic manuscripts. The Rev. James Johnstone translated it word for word from the Flateyan and Frisian manuscripts and added notes. Johnstone served as chaplain to the British envoy at the court of Denmark. His translation was first printed for the author in 1782, and this Edinburgh edition came out in 1882.

The old Norse text tells how a Norwegian fleet sailed against Scotland late in the reign of Haco. For readers of medieval history, the value lies in hearing the campaign from the Norwegian side, in a source written close to the events.
the-old-northwest-a-chronicle-of-the-ohi: Frederic Austin Ogg wrote The Old Northwest, a chronicle of the Ohio Valley and beyond, published by Yale University Press in 1919 as volume 19 of the Chronicles of America series. No chapter text is present here; the opening stops at the front matter and contents. That list opens with Pontiac's Conspiracy and moves through the Revolution, the great migration, and pioneer days, to Tecumseh, the War of 1812, and the Upper Mississippi Valley.
the-open-secret-of-ireland:
T. M. Kettle wrote The Open Secret of Ireland, published in London in 1912, with an introduction by J. E. Redmond, M.P. The contents run from history, coloured and plain, through the obviousness of Home Rule and the ravages of Unionism, to the mechanics of Home Rule and an epilogue on loyalty.

Kettle opens by noting that Ireland again blocks the way after nearly twenty years. Home Rule was rejected by the Commons and the voters in 1886 and by the Lords in 1893, yet the idea survived and grew stronger. An old proverb on the title page warns that the war of Ireland shall never have end without a new remedy.
the-orange-yellow-diamond: J. S. Fletcher published the mystery novel The Orange-Yellow Diamond in 1921. Present here are the front matter and a contents list; the story itself is not among them. The chapter titles still sketch the plot: The Pretty Pawnbroker, Mrs. Goldmark's Eating-House, and The Dead Man open the list. Later chapters name The Platinum Solitaire, The Spanish Manuscript, The Inquest, and Whose Were Those Rings?, promising a London crime tale built around jewels and sudden death.
the-pirates-of-malabar-and-an-englishwom: Colonel John Biddulph's The Pirates of Malabar, with the story of an Englishwoman in India two hundred years ago, was published in 1907. Here only the title pages and the start of the contents appear, so the history itself is absent. Chapter I, on the rise of European piracy in the East, lists Portuguese and Dutch pirates, royal filibustering, and Endymion Porter's venture. It also names the Courten Association, the Indian Red Sea fleet, and the ill feeling raised against the English at Surat.
the-poets-and-poetry-of-cecil-county-mar:
The Poets and Poetry of Cecil County, Maryland, was collected and edited by George Johnston and published by him at Elkton in 1887. Johnston, author of a history of the county, explains in his preface that the volume began as a memorial. Teachers and pupils in the county's northeastern schools wanted to honour the late School Commissioner David Scott. They first planned to raise money for a monument over his grave.

Johnston proposed instead that Scott's poems be collected and published as the best monument he could have. When inquiry showed Scott had not left enough poems for a volume alone, the plan widened. The book now gathers, so far as proved practicable, the writings of all poets native to Cecil County. It adds those who had lived and written there. A verse motto from Herbert heads the title page.
the-red-hand: Arthur Machen is named as author in an Australian electronic edition. The edition was first posted in June 2006. Its heading dates the work to 1895. Five headings are listed for the tales. The first poses a problem of fish-hooks. An incident of a letter follows. A search for a vanished heaven comes next. An artist of the pavement and a treasure-house story close the list. Only the edition header is present here. Those headings appear with it. The tales themselves do not appear.
the-rescue-of-the-princess-winsome-a-fai: Annie Fellows Johnston, author of the Little Colonel books, wrote a fairy play for old and young with music by Albion Fellows Bacon, published at Boston by L. C. Page and Company in 1908 with copyright of 1902. A note explains that songs set with sheet music have been reset as plain lyrics for legibility. Here only the title pages and that note are present, so the play itself does not appear.
the-river-s-end:
James Oliver Curwood opens in the far north, where Mounted Police officer Conniston and outlaw Keith look strikingly alike in face and build. That resemblance breeds a strange confidence between hunter and hunted and tempts Conniston toward betraying his oath.

For twenty-seven months Conniston has pursued Keith under orders to return with his man dead or alive. Now illness strikes in camp: a racking cough, blood on the lips, and Keith supporting the lawman's shoulders without a word. Pursuit turns into dependence at once, and Curwood builds his tale on that reversal.
the-rover-boys-in-camp-or-the-rivals-of-: Dated 1904, The Rover Boys in Camp bears the subtitle The Rivals of Pine Island. Arthur M. Winfield wrote the volume. The surviving portion gives a title page and a thirty-chapter contents list. The text then stops at the heading of chapter one. No narrative follows. The headings trace the boys from home to Putnam Hall. They march to an encampment on Pine Island, where rivals plot mischief. Later entries promise hazers at work and a storm in camp. Dick's midnight adventure and true heroism close the list.
the-shades-of-the-wilderness-a-story-of-: Joseph A. Altsheler's The Shades of the Wilderness bills itself as a story of Lee's great stand. The series list runs from The Guns of Bull Run to The Tree of Appomattox. This volume stands seventh among the eight. The pages shown give that series list and a long roster of principal characters only. Harry Kenton fights on the Southern side, the roster says. His cousin Dick Mason fights on the Northern side. No chapter text follows, so the story itself is not shown here.
the-sky-pilot-in-no-man-s-land:
Ralph Connor's The Sky Pilot in No Man's Land runs to twenty chapters, its contents say. Only a Missionary opens the book. Questions of conscience, rejection, and the war drum's call follow. The men of the north reach France at chapter ten. A man of God, intensive training, and thinning ranks come later. The pilot's last port and Carry On close the list.

Chapter one opens high upon a rock by a river pool. A youth stands poised like a bird for flight, stark naked. His satin skin shines like gold and silver in the rising sun. He gazes into the pool twenty feet below, calculating the distance. A man with a paddle emerges from the bushes and stares in wonder. Ye gods, what a picture, the man says to himself.
the-son-of-my-friend:
T. S. Arthur, author of Ten Nights in a Bar-Room, wrote this short temperance tale, issued in Philadelphia by T. S. Arthur and Son as the first of a series called New Temperance Tales. A wife narrates, and the opening finds her talking with her husband as he draws on his gloves before going out.

She argues that they owe their friends a party after accepting many invitations that winter. He agrees in principle, though work leaves the burden to her, and she proposes hiring a professional caterer to supply everything. Their easy domestic bargaining frames a moral tale from a writer known for fiction against drink.
the-story-of-a-piece-of-coal-what-it-is-:
Edward A. Martin, a fellow of the Geological Society, published this little book in 1896 to tell what coal is, whence it comes, and whither it goes. His preface is dated from Thornton Heath in February 1896. He complains that few people know coal's marvels. He gathers its plant and mineral history into a few pages.

Martin ranges over coal's discovery and early use, its bearing on the great fog problem, its illuminating gas and oils, and the possible exhaustion of British supplies. He marvels at the products drawn from gas-tar. He notes that coal touches many trades. Botanists, geologists, and physicists study it. Chemists, health officers, and merchants deal with it. A contents list then begins with the origin of coal and its plants.
the-story-of-ireland:
Emily Lawless wrote this history for the Story of the Nations series, published in New York and London in 1896 with some additions by Mrs. Arthur Bronson, and dedicated to the Earl of Dufferin. Her preface warns the reader honestly about the road ahead.

Irish history, Lawless says, runs like a long, dark road. Blind alleys branch off it. Sudden turnings and crooked stretches follow. Few sign-posts guide the traveller. Threatening notices stand on either side. The ground hides perils for the unwary. That image frames her task of guiding a general reader through a past she refuses to simplify, beginning with the genuine explorer's confidence and proceeding into the difficulties themselves.
the-story-of-mankind:
Hendrik Van Loon dedicates this history of humanity to Hansje and Willem. He was a professor of the social sciences. His foreword remembers an expedition of his boyhood. An uncle gave him his love of books and pictures. The uncle promised to take the twelve-year-old up Old Saint Lawrence's tower in Rotterdam.

A sexton locked them in with a huge key. It was as large as Saint Peter's own. Silence and darkness met them, floor after floor. They passed a dusty storeroom. It held discarded symbols of a discarded faith. A barren room roosted hundreds of pigeons. That climb, Van Loon implies, taught him how the past is stored above the noise of the present street, the standpoint from which his story of mankind is told.
the-story-of-newfoundland: The Right Hon. the Lord Birkenhead, Lord High Chancellor of Great Britain, wrote this history of Newfoundland, issued in a new and enlarged edition by Horace Marshall and Son in London in 1920. Presented here are a transcriber's note on preserved spellings, the title pages, and the heading of a contents list alone, so Birkenhead's account of the colony itself does not appear.
the-story-of-the-soil-from-the-basis-of-: Cyril G. Hopkins wrote this farming work on the soil. Only the Project Gutenberg etext header appears in this record. It names the title and author. It gives a release date of October 2003 for etext number 4527. The file was first posted in February 2002. Steve Solomon produced it. The archive's standard notices follow. They speak of checking copyright laws and keeping the file intact. No page of Hopkins's book itself is present here.
the-strange-cabin-on-catamount-island: Lawrence J. Leslie wrote this boys' adventure in sixteen chapters. A dare is given first, and Bandy-Legs lands in trouble. The boys explore an island with a bad name. The mystery of a strange cabin follows. Unseen perils and unexpected allies come next. A last camp fire closes the tale. Only the title page and that contents list are present in this record, so the Catamount Island adventure itself does not appear.
the-swiss-family-robinson-or-adventures-:
A preface to this desert-island classic, issued with eight illustrations by John Gilbert, recalls that an English translation of the tale's first part won deserved popularity years earlier. Readers followed the family's slow progress. The family rose from utter destitution to happiness and plenty. Their own labour, perseverance, and obedience won it. Every young reader adopted one boy as a personal acquaintance. Fritz was noble, Ernest studious, and Jack generous.

The original book had one defect: its author's death left it unfinished. The Baroness de Montolieu supplied the conclusion, sanctioned by the author's son, and this edition re-translates the whole for an English family circle. An introduction then frames the tale as fact, telling how Counsellor Horner, sailing with Captain Krusenstern, found a German-speaking family of parents and four sons on a fertile island south-west of Java.
the-teacher-moral-influences-employed-in:
Jacob Abbott's Teacher, in a new and revised edition dated 1873, sets out a system for organizing and governing a school through moral influences rather than force. His preface explains that he offers no new theories. Instead he develops principles that skillful, experienced teachers already admit and act upon, and carries them into practical detail. The book aims at beginners who want to borrow the experience of others.

Abbott adds that a teacher's power over pupils' minds and hearts should rest chiefly on moral influence. His calm, methodical preface promises classroom arrangements, motives, and discipline handled without harshness. Generations of American teachers learned their craft from Abbott, and this manual shows his steady belief that character, not fear, runs a good school.
the-thirsty-sword-a-story-of-the-norse-i:
Robert Leighton set The Thirsty Sword during the Norse invasion of Scotland in 1262 and 1263, opening on a June evening above a stream on Bute. A girl in grey homespun and a crimson silk girdle walks restlessly, wishing Kenric were here. She looks toward Kilinory castle across the moor, with Arran's blue mountains southward and Kintyre's hills catching the sunset. A dead capercailzie, an arrow in its breast, thuds onto the heather at her feet.

Kenric himself bounds from the trees with his longbow, a hare and moor fowl at his belt, surprised to find Ailsa alone so late. He is sixteen, broad, strong, and ruddy from sea air. Leighton launches a boy's adventure of love, loyalty, and coming war with the Norsemen.
the-vikings-of-helgeland: Henrik Ibsen's Vikings of Helgeland, dated 1858, appears in William Archer's translation within the third volume of Ibsen's prose dramas. The pages present here give the cast list and staging notes, so the play's dialogue does not appear. Action is set around A. D. 933, in the time of Erik Blood-axe, at Gunnar's house on Helgeland in northern Norway. Characters include Ornulf of the Fiords, an Icelandic chieftain, Sigurd the Strong, a sea-king, and Gunnar, a rich yeoman. Dagny is Ornulf's daughter and Hiordis his foster-daughter.
the-visionary-pictures-from-nordland: Jonas Lie's Visionary, or Pictures from Nordland, reached English readers in Jessie Muir's translation, published by Hodder Brothers in London in 1894. A preface and a portrait of the author are promised on the title page. The material present here is the title page and contents, so Lie's story itself does not appear. Contents divide the volume into an introduction, a section on Nordland and its people, and eleven chapters. Headings run from Home and On the Shore through the servants' hall, confirmation, and a storm.
the-way-of-the-wind: Zoë Anderson Norris, author of The Color of His Soul, published The Way of the Wind with what the title page calls her own publishing house in New York. She lists herself as writer, editor, and publisher, noting she is a native of Kentucky living in the East. The pages present here give the title pages and a start of contents, so Norris's text does not appear. One visible chapter title, A Free Lecture, follows a dedication to her little brother in acknowledgement of a debt unpaid.
the-well-at-the-worlds-end:
William Morris wrote this vast quest tale in four books, and it came out in 1896. It is the longest of the prose romances of his last years. Morris built a whole made up world for it, with its own lands, towns, and tongues of speech.

Ralph of Upmeads leaves home to seek the well whose water grants a long and hale life. Kings, witches, and a fair maid mark his road through a rich, strange world of romance. The book taught Tolkien and Lewis the craft of world building, and its sway is still felt.
the-young-emigrants-madelaine-tube-the-b: A Scribner volume from 1851 bundles four children's works, and its opening contents are what appear here. The Young Emigrants leads the collection. Madelaine Tube, The Boy and the Book, and The Crystal Palace follow. The first tale's chapters promise sights at sea and the New World. Illustrations accompanied the original edition for young readers. The stories themselves begin beyond the pages present in this record.
this-is-the-end:
Stella Benson published her novel in 1917 and opens with a narrator who distrusts all systems and reasons. Hands were made to grope, she says, and only unaccountable things can be counted on. A policeman growing wings would not truly surprise her.

She introduces Jay, a bus conductor and idealist, while denying that any heroine exists here. Jay questions every rule, from being good to crossing her legs above the knee, and sleeps still waiting for a better answer. Readers get a whimsical, sceptical story where certainty itself is the target.
through-the-mackenzie-basin-a-narrative-: Charles Mair narrated the Athabasca and Peace River treaty expedition of 1899 through the Mackenzie Basin. He inscribed the record to the Hon. David Laird, who led the expedition and was his old friend. Chapter one travels from Edmonton to Lesser Slave Lake past peat beds, a gas well, boats, and trackers. Chapter two adds rapids, missionary celebrations, hay meadows, and a dangerous squall. Chapter three reaches treaty proceedings with named chiefs. Only the contents summaries are present here, so Mair's narrative itself is not shown.
tis-sixty-years-since-address-of-charles:
Charles Francis Adams delivered his Founders' Day address on January 16, 1913, taking his title from the subtitle of Walter Scott's Waverley. Scott's novel, published in 1814, looked back sixty years to the Stuart rising of 1745. Adams entered Harvard in 1853, exactly sixty years before his speech.

He argues that school life ends and thinking, acting life begins at a university's threshold. Scott had died only twenty years before his college days, and Tennyson's Locksley Hall spoke directly to his generation. Readers get an elder statesman's compressed one-hour retrospect on education, literature, and a changing century.
tom-tiddler-s-ground:
Charles Dickens's Christmas story opens at an inn parlour, where a traveller eating chops and tea asks why the place bears its odd name. The landlord explains that a local man scatters halfpence to tramps on his own land, like the children's game where players snatch coins. The man, Mr. Mopes, is called a hermit.

Pressed to define a hermit, the landlord stalls, and the traveller supplies his own verdict: an abominably dirty, intolerably conceited thing. The landlord concedes each point in careful, evasive phrases. Readers get Dickens dialogue built from politeness, gossip, and quiet insult.
travels-in-syria-and-the-holy-land:
John Lewis Burckhardt's Travels in Syria and the Holy Land appeared in 1822 under the African Association's name. The editor's preface explains why a society devoted to African discovery published Asian travels. Burckhardt had been hired to prepare for a mission into Africa's interior.

He spent nearly three years at Aleppo learning Arabic language and manners well enough to pass as a Muslim traveller. His Syrian tours took him through districts Europeans seldom visited, adding fresh knowledge of the country's geography. Blocked from Africa after reaching Egypt, he spent five more years travelling nearby lands. The preface frames the journals that follow as the fruit of that long preparation.
trevelyan-garibaldi-thousand:
Garibaldi and the Thousand, from 1909, forms the trilogy's middle book. Trevelyan recounts the bold 1860 landing of red-shirted men in Sicily. One thousand volunteers sail to take a kingdom held by an army.

Against steep odds, the Thousand win town after town by daring. Garibaldi's calm in crisis steadies men who should have failed fast. Trevelyan mixes a scholar's care with a poet's fire in the telling. He makes readers feel dust, heat, and hope on the march north. The campaign that made Italy reads here as pure, true adventure story. Trevelyan's maps and marches keep the daring drive clear throughout.
trooper-peter-halket-of-mashonaland:
Olive Schreiner's Trooper Peter Halket of Mashonaland, in a colonial edition dated February 1897, opens with a grim photograph described in words. Three black men hang from a tree in Matabeleland while eight white men stand by, untroubled. Schreiner dedicates the book to Sir George Grey, once governor of the Cape Colony.

Her dedication praises Grey's uncorruptible justice and broad humanity toward Dutch, English, and native alike. A short glossary explains veld, kraal, riem, and Cape smoke for English readers. Chapter one places Peter Halket alone by a fire on a kopje on a dark, starless night. The tale indicts chartered-company rule in Rhodesia through one trooper's night of reckoning.
twilight-land:
Howard Pyle's Twilight Land opens with the storyteller already inside that country, unable to say how he arrived. No sun scorches there, no rain muddies the road, and no wind blows dust into a traveller's eyes. All is sweet and quiet and ready for bed.

Pyle drifts along the high-road like a soap bubble before the wind, past trees, bushes, and the mill-pond. Birds sing their good-night song and frogs pipe in the purple-gray dusk. The contents promise sixteen tales, from The Stool of Fortune and The Talisman of Solomon to The Salt of Life. The introduction casts the whole book as a walk into a storyteller's dusk.
under-the-southern-cross-or-travels-in-a: Maturin Murray Ballou's Under the Southern Cross, dated 1888, promises travels in Australia, Tasmania, New Zealand, Samoa, and other Pacific islands. The pages present here are publisher's advertisements for Ballou's other travel books, chiefly Due North. They are filled with long quotes from newspapers. The travel narrative itself does not appear in these pages. Reviewers quoted in the ads call Ballou a model traveller. They praise his ease, his good humor, and his gift for mixing instruction with entertainment. Reading him, one paper says, comes close to making the trip.
unknown-to-history-a-story-of-the-captiv:
Charlotte M. Yonge's Unknown to History, dated 1882, retells the captivity of Mary Queen of Scots as a novel. Her preface names the sources she worked from: a report printed in Strickland's life of the queen and in Burton's history of Scotland. She admits she trimmed the Babington plot and dropped many real attendants, since a full account would have tangled the tale.

Chapters listed here run past the opening set found in a twin record of the same book, reaching a furious letter at chapter twelve. Titles along the way include The Lady Arbell, Queen Mary's Presence Chamber, and The Key of the Cipher. Both records share the same preface; this one's contents simply extend further. The story mixes a found child, secret letters, and court intrigue around the imprisoned queen.
up-in-ardmuirland:
The Rev. Michael Barrett, a Benedictine monk, wrote Up in Ardmuirland. Benziger Brothers issued the book in 1912. His contents promise a year of Scottish country life in twelve chapters. They name memories, a boy called Archie, golden dreams, and a schoolmaster, Dominie Dick. Smugglers, spring's return, a rustic pastor, and a sprig of shamrock follow. The book opens with a poem tag from Longfellow's Miles Standish, about forest, meadow, hill, and the rim of the sea.

Chapter one, called Personal, introduces the narrator and his twin brother Val. The two have always been treated as inseparable. Life has often forced them apart, yet they drift back to the old companionship nature seemed to intend. Barrett writes as a priest looking back on a parish world he knew well. Readers get gentle sketches of rural Scotland. Family memory and local character carry them, rather than plot.
vanishing-england: P. H. Ditchfield wrote Vanishing England, issued by Methuen at London in 1910 with pictures by Fred Roe. The pages given here hold the title page and the start of the contents, so the chapters themselves are not shown. Early chapter titles promise an introduction, the disappearance of England, old walled towns, streets and lanes, old castles, churches that are vanishing or gone, and old mansions. A later chapter takes up the ruin of prehistoric remains. The frontispiece shows the George Inn at Norton St. Philip in Somerset.
walter-harland:
H. S. Caswell, author of Clara Boscom and Earnest Harwood, wrote Walter Harland, or Memories of the Past, in 1874. Chapter one finds the narrator alone on a quiet afternoon, in the soft haze of Indian summer in eastern Canada. The stillness sets his thoughts wandering into the dreamy regions of the past, and scenes long gone, almost forgotten, pass in review before his mind's eye.

Musing so, he forms a plan. Few lives, however humble or obscure, would lack all interest if their history were noted down in a book. Like a boy who has dreamed a remarkable dream and cannot tell where to begin, he puzzles over his start, then sets to the work. Readers get a Canadian life recalled in old age, offered in the plain faith that common experience, honestly kept, is worth a stranger's hour.
war-is-kind:
Stephen Crane published War Is Kind in 1899, with drawings by Will Bradley. The book holds poems built on a bitter refrain. The title poem speaks to a maiden, a babe, and a mother in turn. It tells each of them not to weep, since war is kind. Between those verses stand the facts the refrain mocks. A lover threw wild hands toward the sky, as his horse ran on alone. A father tumbled in the yellow trenches. A field lies where a thousand corpses rest.

Crane calls the men of the regiment little souls who thirst for fight, born to drill and die. He bids the blazing flag make plain to them the virtue of slaughter. A second piece asks a shell on the shore what the sea says, and hears of a brother long silent. The poems are short, hard, and musical.
what-s-the-matter-with-ireland:
Ruth Russell published What's the Matter with Ireland? in 1920. She gave the book to her mother. Its contents cover Sinn Fein, Irish labor, and the role of the Catholic Church. One chapter studies the peaceful plan of the writer known as AE. Belfast gets a chapter of its own.

A letter printed up front, dated January 29, 1920, praises Russell's speed in grasping Irish views. It comes from the American group for the elected government of the Irish Republic. The writer hopes her first chapter will correct false cries of Irish wealth. Russell went to see the land herself, and the book reports what she found.
whosoever-shall-offend: F. Marion Crawford's novel Whosoever Shall Offend is shown here by its title page, a verse, and a list of pictures, with the tale only just begun. Horace T. Carpenter drew eight pictures in Rome at Crawford's direction for the 1905 book. The title quotes Christ on harm done to little ones who believe. The picture list names a sleeping death, a girl with a copper vessel, and Ercole leaving home at sunset. Chapter one begins as a widow marries young Corbario.
wit-without-money-a-comedy-the-works-of-:
Wit Without Money is a comedy from the works of Francis Beaumont and John Fletcher. The cast list names Valentine, a gallant who will not be talked into keeping his estate. His younger brother Francisco and their uncle, Master Lovegood, stand near him. A widow, Lady Hartwell, draws three suitors from Valentine's circle.

Act one opens with the uncle and a merchant friend. The merchant asks when he last saw Valentine. Not since the horse race, the uncle says; the young man is taken up with men who woo the widow. A clown servant, a falconer, and musicians fill out the cast. Spendthrift wit, debt, and a rich widow drive the comedy.
withered-leaves-from-memory-s-garland: Abigail Stanley Hanna published this verse and prose gathering in 1857. Pages present here show the title page, a short motto about voices from past years, and an index of pieces. The index names memories of an old homestead, a schoolhouse, and a graveyard. It also lists midnight scenes, a household history, poems on illness, and a scene on the Kennebec River. The pieces themselves do not appear in these pages.
wylder-s-hand: J. Sheridan Le Fanu published this novel in 1864. Pages present here give a chapter list, but no chapter text. Early titles follow a ride through Gylingden village with Mark Wylder's letter in hand. Later titles name Dorcas Brandon, Captain Stanley Lake, a pony carriage, and a Persian magician's ring. A country house party and a missing man seem central, judging by the titles. The story itself does not begin in these pages.
young-folks-history-of-england: Charlotte M. Yonge wrote this history of England for young readers. Pages present here hold a contents list covering twenty chapters, but no chapter text. The chapters run from Julius Caesar in 55 B. C. through the Romans, the Danish conquest, and the Normans. Kings then follow in order, from William the Conqueror to Henry V. Each chapter title pairs a ruler with dates. The narrative itself does not appear in these pages.
young-folks-library-volume-xi-of-20-wond: Thomas Bailey Aldrich led the editors of this twenty-volume Young Folks' Library, in a third edition dated 1902. Volume eleven covers wonders of earth, sea, and sky. Pages present here hold series title pages and the editorial board list, but no selections. Board members include former navy secretary John D. Long and nature writer Ernest Thompson Seton. The readings themselves, drawn from many lands, do not appear in these pages.
